ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should reinstate core funding for women's centres, to enable those centres to continue to provide essential information, referral and support services to women.
She said: Madam Speaker, this is a very important motion on a very important issue. The devastation to women's centres by this latest budget cut really speaks to not only a lack of fiscal support for women's centres but a concerted political effort on the part of this government to silence the voice of dissent of women across Canada.
Women's centres grew out of the recommendations of the 1970 Royal Commission on the Status of Women. That royal commission spoke of the real inequality that women faced in our country. The recommendations of the royal commission were being implemented gradually, painfully slowly, across Canada. Women's centres were playing a significant role in this process.
Women's centres are necessary. Some of the services that they provide include services for battered women who do not know where to turn, where the nearest shelter is, or how to get there, or even which lawyers they would best talk to. Women's centres provide that information and sometimes they are adjacent to the very services which a battered woman would require.
Teenage women get information regarding sexuality or sexually transmitted diseases and the location of supportive health centres. Women's centres provide that information. There are homeless women right here in Ottawa. The Women's Place in Ottawa has operated as a drop-in centre for homeless women on weekends because there was a gap in social services provided by municipal and other services.
The centres can tell jobless women, newly divorced women, young women, or older women who may not know where to start looking for a job what job programs are available for them and can provide counselling.
Centres inform mothers and parents what child care facilities are available in a community; they advise immigrant and visible minority women what programs are available to them, what organizations can help them.
Women's centres can help sexually harassed women and those who are discriminated against at work, by telling them what the law says, and explaining their rights. Many have a list of lawyers who can help them.
All women and men in a community can use the resources of a women's centre. They provide public information and public education on women's issues. They speak out on matters affecting women.
With these latest cuts, 100 per cent of their core funding, these services are going to be at least drastically reduced if not eliminated completely in some cases. That is going to have a very negative impact for the kind of work we have tried to do over the years to implement the recommendations of that Royal commission report.
For example, in Whitehorse, cuts to women's and to native organizations' funding means a cut to 80 per cent of the voluntary organizations in the Yukon. This is a pattern that has evolved over time.
The Secretary of State's women's program was cut in the 1989-90 budget by $2 million. In the last budget it was cut by a further $1.6 million.

April 6, 1990

At the same time, the argument is that we have to address our deficit. I think there is no one in this House who is going to deny that the deficit has to be addressed and reduced, but the debate is about the way in which that is being done.
In this same budget that reduced the core funding for over 75 women's centres by 100 per cent, there were increases as well. There was an increase to the budget for CSIS in the amount of $33 million. There were also $14 million allocated for advertising for the GST. We can see where the priorities of the government are. When you consider $33 million for CSIS and $14 million for advertising for the GST, $1.6 million is a very small amount, and one wonders how credible the argument is that this is a cut that is necessary to reduce the deficit.
It is also very interesting that it comes at a time when this government has been spoken to very forcefully by the women of Canada in their opposition to the initiatives under Bill C-43, the recriminalization of abortion. I do not believe that it is just a coincidence.
I think there is a political agenda that is being followed here. The voices of women from those women's centres and their ability to do organizing in communities has been profoundly limited by these budget cuts. What is happening now is that those women's centres are now having to redirect their energies by fundraising, in order to keep their centres open and in order to do project analyses and write up project proposals.
Having been the Chair of the board of our local women's centre in Victoria, I know the kind of energy that has to be put into that paperwork. The staff of those women's centres are often paid very little. They are dependent upon volunteer work as well. I know the staff of our women's centre in Victoria was paid about $22,000 a year, which is probably the national average.
One does not work in those centres in order to get rich. One works there because of the hope that ultimately the recommendations from the Royal commission's report of 1970 will come to fruition and that there will be real equality for women in Canada. Those women staffers, right from Victoria to Newfoundland, are committed women who are doing the government's work at a very low wage. They are doing it with commitment and passion. It is a very effective way of trying to implement what the government itself has set out. So, again the
argument that the cut of the $1.6 million is a deficit reduction initiative falls flat.
There is another agenda here. The agenda is to silence women, but I can tell you that women will not be silenced. We have seen, throughout the week, the initiatives of women who will not be silenced. We have seen them from Newfoundland to Port Alberni and to the north.
The 100 per cent cut to core funding for the women's resource centre in Whitehorse, in the Yukon, means that that centre will have to close its doors. The closest women's centre, if that is closed, is in Port Coquitlam, British Columbia. Is that what the government means by alternatives?
What are we going to do? Are we to pay air fare for women to come and consult? Are we to pay long distance phone charges? No.
The reason that these funds are being reduced is to silence women, and women will not be silenced. It fits in with this government's agenda to silence the poor of Canada. The poor will not be silenced.
My colleague from Mission-Coquitlam, in her duty as social policy critic, has met with a number of low income women and low income men who are dependent on social services. These are the kinds of people we should be looking after.
It really speaks about the role of government when we talk about cuts to women's programs. Who are we supposed to be helping through our taxation system? Is it the people that are already doing well enough? The government seems to think so. The cuts to women's centres, native centres and other initiatives can make the government uncomfortable. I think it is a quite blatant political act to keep them quiet.
I would like to turn to the effect of the closure of centres. In British Columbia the following women's centres are about to close: the women's centres in Chetwynd, Fort St. John, Howe Sound, Kelowna, Penticton, Port Alberni, and Kitimat.
We have asked repeatedly to meet with the minister responsible, the Secretary of State. He has sent officials with no power to make changes to the funding situation. These officials further angered the women, and I think the minister responsible has also incurred their wrath. Last Monday, the women members of our caucus sent a
April 6, 1990

letter to the minister asking for a meeting at his convenience. We have not received a response.
This is an urgent situation, and that is why we are using this opposition day to put forth this motion. I think it is a black mark on this government if it feels it can get away with this, and there will be continuing civil disobedience if it is to continue.
We should also focus on the fact that the government's international reputation will be sullied by this action. The government is breaking international treaties by this initiative. Canada has signed the UN convention for the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women. The government has also gone along with the Nairobi forward looking strategies.
Canada cannot say one thing in international fora and another thing at home. We are talking about $1.6 million dollars, a piddling amount when we consider some of the other initiatives that have been increased by this government in what is being applauded as a deficit reducing budget. Canadians are not fooled at all.
In responding to questions on the committee for the elimination of discrimination against women about the country's success in combating discrimination against women, the permanent representation of Canada at the United Nations explained that it was the strength of the Canadian feminist movement and the commitment of Canada's leaders to the equal rights for women. How does eliminating the core funding for women's centres demonstrate the commitment to equal rights for women? There may be some painful logic, and I am willing to listen to it today.
The women's movement is constantly undermined by funding cuts and the refusal by government to meet with the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, Canada's largest women's lobby group, made up of over 600 women's organizations. Not only has this budget cut $1.6 million from women's centres funding, it has also cut funds available to feminist publications. I think that is also a concerted effort to reduce the ability of those publications to work effectively and to bring the women's agenda to light. There is a concerted attack on women's equality through those reductions. I remind the

House that this is a cut of $1.6 million, compared to a $33 million increase for the budget of CSIS.
That comparison alone speaks to the government's agenda, of this government's priority, and of its lack of commitment to promoting the equality of women. It is a black day if this government continues with this initiative. I hope the minister responsible will go back to his cabinet colleagues. I also hope the Minister responsible for the Status of Women will carry out her responsibilities for the status of women and will ask her cabinet colleagues, as my motion indicates, that the funds be reinstated for those women's centres so that the women of Canada, from Newfoundland to British Columbia, to Yukon, to Yellowknife, will be able to do their work as they have done in a a very efficient, effective, low cost and committed way.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words today concerning women's centres in relation to comments that the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands has made.
Some 10 years ago in Scarborough we set up a women's centre. I was a member of the board founding that centre. It was very important to establish the centre in order to reach out to women who are having difficulty so that we could as sisters help them. In the process of setting up that women's centre we looked for funds. We spent a lot of time around the table filling in those applications, getting the right words in order that the funding would become available, but at no time did we believe 10 years ago that our sole funding for women's centres was to be from the federal government.
At that time we were looking to foundations, to the community, and to fund raising events to see how we could have funding from various levels. I am very pleased today, thanks to two very wonderful individuals in Scarborough, Nina Willcocks and Linda Davis, who have diversified this funding so that now there is very little funding from various levels of government in order to provide services for social justice and economic equality for the women in Scarborough.

April 6, 1990
Supply
I have a question and comment. The hon. member speaks about funding cuts. Let us look at some of the numbers. In 1984-85, the year just before the Conservative Party took over the government, the funding was about $8 million for women's programs under Secretary of State. There has been a tremendous increase in that funding. In 1988-89 it was $13 million.
The commitment demonstrated by a number of women within our own party in order to increase funding dramatically over the last six years is a great credit to the government and these women. Many have benefited from those programs.
I think that it is time that we started setting some of the record straight in terms of the advantages we have been able to provide for /omen, such as jobs and the number of women who have been able to establish their own businesses. Two-thirds of the businesses in Canada started in the last six years have been started by women.
I wanted to set the record straight. I look forward to doing so as we progress through this debate.

Madam Speaker, it is a very good idea to set the record straight. Let me begin my remarks by setting the record straight regarding the 1990-91 commitment for women. The women's program has been cut to $9 million from $13 million. We are back nearly to 1984-85 levels. When we take inflation into account, that shows the real commitment to women's centres.
We should really address what the government is trying to do by having women focus on fund raising. Every minute used to raise funds is a minute taken away from organizing and creating real change in Canada. Do not think that women are fooled. They are not.

I would like to direct a question to my colleague. How does she explain to the people at women centres that there is no money from the federal government, while at the same time it can find $16 million to spend on a GST that is going to be detrimental to women and their families and is not supported by 80 per cent of Canadian population? does she explain to women this tremendous contradiction in the Tory government policy?

I think the women and men of Canada have seen through the pained logic that this is going to assist in reducing the deficit and have seen that this is a concerted political act to silence women. I do not try to explain the kind of logic that will allow for $14 million in advertising for the GST, which as my colleague points out is going to be hurting the very women and men the centres are trying to assist.
The redistributive capacity of our tax system is at stake here. We are talking about what the government should be doing with our money and the kind of initiatives that this government has undertaken since it gained office again in 1988. It has spoken very clearly about the kind of direction it believes it should take.
The women and the women's centres have voiced very clearly their opposition to the government's agenda. I think that is one of the reasons for this latest round of cuts. The government is using these cuts to silence women.

Madam Speaker, I happen to be the member of Parliament for the riding of Mission-Coquitlam where the Port Coquitlam women's centre is located. To set the record straight, I would like to tell hon. members that 100 per cent of funding is not expected by that woman's centre or any other women's centre from this government.
I would like to ask hon. members in this House to consider information about the monetary value of the volunteer time put into women's centres.
The volunteer time amounts to 2,700 hours. If we multiply that by $10.50 an hour, which is the average hourly wage paid to counsellors across the country, we see it equals $28,350. That is how much our collective time as women is worth.
If we multiply the $28,350 figure by the 33 women's centres in British Columbia we get $935,550, almost double what it would cost to keep these centres open.
In setting the record straight, we have to remember that women are putting in $935,550 for centres that

Over the course of the last few days I have watched with dismay as misleading reports obscured the simple truth of the matter. The motion before the House on the issue of funding to women's centres gives me the opportunity to speak to all members and through them to all Canadians.

This year, for example, we will be working with over 550 voluntary women's organizations building a vital partnership in every province and territory. For example, we have made a priority of programs which assist immigrant and visible minority women, women with disabilities and native women. We have assisted women's groups in improving their fundraising skills.

We are addressing the problem of family violence with a multi-year strategy that is giving concrete results. We have taken a government-wide approach, calling on the resources of my department and those of Health and Welfare, Indian and Northern Affairs and Justice, as well as Canada Mortgage and Housing.

We have responded to the issue of family violence with a budget of over $40 million, including some $22.5 million for CMHC's Project Haven which will provide 500 shelter units for women and children. But our commitment goes beyond funding.
The government has built up an impressive legislative record with amendments to the Canada Pension Plan, to the Pension Benefits Standards Act, to the Old Age
Security Act, to the Indian Act and it enacted the first national Employment Equity Act. The list goes on and on.
The government has more than doubled the number of women appointed to federal boards, agencies and commissions.
The government has increased the number of women working at the deputy minister level from seven in 1984 to 21 today.
We have everything to be proud of, so I find pathetic the litany of gloom I hear from across the way. Let them measure their record against ours. I know what the outcome will be.

When the Prime Minister appointed me Secretary of State, he gave me the mission to do what I could to make equality a reality for all Canadians. Needless to say, real equality must include the group which makes up more than half the population of this country: Canadian women. That is exactly what the government has been doing over the past six years. We have done more for equality than any government before us.
Nevertheless, in hard times, one must make hard decisions. We cannot avoid them. The people of this country expect the government to be responsible.
As part of the government-wide expenditure reduction measures, my department's women's program budget was reduced from $11.2 million to $9.6 million. This reduction was part of an across-the-board effort affecting many departments. We simply must make sacrifices now to be able tomorrow to have the strong Canada we all desire.

I have instructed my officials to deal with these applications on an urgent basis. For years some 20 centres across the country have been securing project funding from my department. With this assistance they have carried out excellent work and made a significant contribution to their communities.

I cannot repeat often enough how important it is for the government to see women's groups diversify their funding. The Women's Program is not the sole source of financial assistance. Other federal departments such as National Health and Welfare, Employment and Immigration, Labour Canada, Justice and the Solicitor General's Department provide assistance as well.
Many provincial governments also appropriate funds for this purpose. Furthermore, an increasing number of
Supply
women's groups are funded by other programs at the Department of the Secretary of State, including Multi-culturalism, Official Languages, Native Women and Disabled Persons Participation.
My department's Women's Program is intended to help women's organizations that are working to promote equality. Let me assure you that the centres will continue to receive assistance for any specific projects that are eligible.
The program has never directly funded health or social services. I want to make it quite clear that the Women's Program is not, and has never been, responsible for subsidizing shelters for battered women. Consequently, the decision with respect to funding for women's centres does not affect battered women, since this type of service is not included in the program's terms of reference.

The fact is that these vital services for some of the most disadvantaged Canadian women are funded at the municipal or provincial levels with the assistance of other federal government departments.
I want to be very clear about this. It is not within the mandate of the women's program of the Secretary of State to fund services for sexual assault victims or rape crisis centres. This program has never had a mandate to provide these kinds of services. It was not created for this purpose.
I would also like to make it clear that the majority of women's centres have survived in this country without core funding from the women's program.
What kinds of projects are funded by the women's program? Let me give you some examples. There are single mothers working to improve their economic opportunities; rural women developing information networks; immigrant women enhancing their skills; voluntary organizations working on child care issues; and women with disabilities organizing workshops on violence.
These few examples give the true flavour of the women's program. It is a program that meets contemporary challenges by assisting women and their organizations. This government takes its responsibility to fund women's centres across the country very seriously.

I have indicated that as quickly as applications can be completed, I will make sure that those applications are fast-tracked so that the money can be flowing to the centres. I am not sure what more anyone could expect, but I think that the individuals who have the concern of the women's centres at heart and the women's program should do all they can to help these initiatives come forward.
These are not easy issues for any one of us, and I know how concerned all members of Parliament are that we do the right thing.
What is interesting is that there is a very important program available through the Secretary of State. As I have indicated, within the Department of Multicultural-ism and Citizenship, we have made available almost $1 million through the program to immigrant women and visible minorities. There is over $2 million in the aboriginal women's program. There is increased funding for the disabled persons' program, and we know that almost 65 per cent of disabled people are women.
It is very important as we look at the over-all capacity of my ministry to respond to the growing needs of women in finally addressing the inequalities of the society that we be given the opportunity to help our client groups.
One thing that has been recognized has been the very positive and effective role that the staff and officials have always played in terms of their desire and their ability to serve their clients. It has been recognized by the people we serve that we have been easy to work with and that we have tried to be helpful wherever we could. This is the message that my regional people have tried to get out.
My associate undersecretary spent three or four days in Newfoundland attempting to help the several women's centres there bring forward their applications. I sense an openness on their part to come together, an openness to see how the project and the program funding can help them carry on.
What is even more important is that I see for the first time, a willingness on the part of Canadians from coast to coast to come together to make sure these important
April 6, 1990

initiatives are allowed to carry on for the benefit of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I invite all the heckling they can muster on the other side of the House, if it makes them feel better. It certainly makes me feel better.
I would like to ask the minister some questions and, again, I would also like to set the record straight. When I have completed I would appreciate it if the minister would tell me how he expects women's centres to utilize program funding when they don't have core funding to pay the rent.
I would also like to point out to the minister that women's centres received five weeks' notice before their core funding was completely cut off. Five weeks is not nearly enough time to replace tens of thousands of dollars of funding. It is evident that obviously this government could not care less what happens to these centres.
The minister gave us a long list of the things that this government has done for women. I would like to talk a little bit about what this government has done for women lately.
I would like to talk about the fact that it reneged on its promise of a new child care system.
It proposed a recriminalization of abortion and removing women's reproductive choice.
It has called a .5 cent reduction in the wage gap between women and men a victory of the employment and equity legislation.
It has proposed a 7 per cent goods and services tax on everything from postage, books, tampons, haircuts, movies to transportation.
It has traded away women's jobs in the electronics, food processing and textiles industries.
It has backed out of its responsibility for unemployment insurance.
It has provided funding for the building of transition houses and shelters, but provided no assurance that there will be funding for programs.
Supply
It shut women out of the consultation decision-making process.
It spent more money on loans to strip clubs than to women's groups.
It continues with an immigration policy which favours rich men, and it continues to discriminate against immigrant women in federally funded language training programs.
It has refused to fund women's work on reproductive choice, lesbian rights and the environment and peace.
It has decreased funding for women's groups in the last two years by $3.6 million.
This government, I am sure, is very proud of that record.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, April 7 is World Health Day. This year, the theme will be health and the environment, and the slogan: "Think globally, act locally".
Together many countries throughout the world, Canada will continue to examine the extremely complex relationship between the environment and public health-whether we are talking about air or water pollution, the quality of food or promoting safe use of chemical products.
As a society, we have learned the hard way that we cannot go beyond certain limits without endangering our own health and that of other living creatures.
I would ask you and your constituents to stop and think a moment about your priorities. Are we doing enough? I
would say that in many cases we are not. Let's not just dream about a healthy environment. Let's make it happen.

Madam Speaker, my colleague, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, and I would like to congratulate the staff of the Cornwall management area office upon receiving Employment and Immigration Canada's 1989 Outstanding Team Award in the management area category in recognition of their excellent work and valuable contribution to the communities in this region.
The team, led by manager Denis Thibault, has met or surpassed project goals and targets for the last three years, consistently keeping within their budget while providing a client service built on dedication and respect for both employers and the available workforce. The team motto is "Our commitment is service", and they have certainly proved that.
The office installed computerized systems to upgrade operations in the employment, insurance, claims and administration sections and created an extensive catalogue of employers and data on the job market. This led to increased job placements and better service for workers requiring assistance.
On behalf of the people of Stormont-Dundas and Glengany-Prescott-Russell, we wish to thank the team and congratulate them on a job well done.

Madam Speaker, this country is once again facing a period in our history when we are all being called upon to be show tolerance and understanding of our fellow Canadians.
During the next several months we will attempt to amend our Constitution to take another step forward in the development of the Canadian nation. We are not taking the last step forward. This is not the end of the process of constitutional renewal. We must all refrain from taking rash or negative actions. It is a time for building on the progress that has already been made. It is not the time to destroy the work of others.

April 6, 1990
I am looking forward to the next few months as all Canadians productively put forward their views on the constitutional renewal of Canada.

Madam Speaker, as the B.C. newspaper The Province put it yesterday, the only thing certain about the Meme breast implant is that doctors and scientists are uncertain about it. At least five scientists in the Department of National Health and Welfare urge that the implant be withdrawn from the market.
The minister claims the Meme is safe on the basis of the Kerrigan report, yet yesterday the minister acknowledged that even Dr. Kerrigan believes that further studies are warranted to address the possible degradation and contents of the foam. This is the main concern and no one seems to be able to say the foam is safe when implanted into the human body.
I am not fearmongering as the minister has suggested. I am trying to get answers to critical questions. Surgitek of Montreal is the only Canadian distributor of this product. The foam itself is imported from Pennsylvania and since 1984, 12,000 implants of this particular product have taken place, 10,000 of those implants in the province of Quebec alone.
I urge the minister to order the withdrawal from the market of the Meme until safety has been proven.

Only 21 of 167 Conservative members are needed to vote with the combined opposition parties to defeat the tax. We urge Canadians across the country to phone their Conservative members of Parliament, raise this issue with them and tell them they oppose the tax.

Madam Speaker, April 7 is World Health Day. This year the theme is "Health and the Environment".
Recent environmental disasters such as the Hagers-ville tire fire emphasize the need for all countries to examine and begin to address the environmental hazards that may pose continuing health problems for future generations of Canadians.
Canada is in an enviable position with its high standard of living, its excellent health and social services system and its incredible supply of natural resources. But we all know that no country can afford to be complacent. We must work hard to preserve what we have and ensure that our environment is a positive force for healthy living.
I would urge you all, both as individual Canadians and as members in your own communities, to think globally and act locally, and to urge your friends, your families and your constituents to do the same.

Madam Speaker, I rise again to bring to the attention of this House the reaction of Canadians of the Islamic faith to current public usage of the term "Islamic terrorism", in particular with reference to an academic conference scheduled to take place this month at the University of Manitoba.
Although I am fairly sure that this phrase was not developed to deliberately insult or demean the Islamic faith, and although this unfortunate term has been used in other parts of the world and in connection with published works, it should be clear to us in Canada that this term derives from insensitivity and ignorance. For example, terrorism in an Islamic country is not more
April 6, 1990

Islamic than terrorism in northern Ireland is Catholic, or terrorism in Israel is Jewish.
Our continuing challenge in Canada and elsewhere in the world is to enhance our inter-cultural and inter-religious sensitivity and respect.
I am pleased to note that organizers of the conference on terrorism are incorporating into that conference a session which will reflect the principles of peace and brotherhood which underlie the Islamic faith.

Madam Speaker, many fishermen and plant workers, both men and women, have not been able to obtain unemployment insurance benefits this winter because the Liberal senators delayed approval of Bill C-21.
The non-elected Liberal appointed senators used all kinds of tactics to block this important legislation, preventing the application of the new measures included in the bill.
Who suffered and are still suffering? Certainly not the Liberal appointed senators, certainly not the Liberal opposition members, but the people living in 15 fishing communities on the lower north shore. They are the ones suffering because of that injustice.
These hard working and decent people are asking the Liberal senators: Why the delaying tactics? They want to know why they are held hostage because of political partisanship. They tell me that they are fed up with partisan politics being carried out on their backs. They want this bill to go through.

Madam Speaker, tourism is the largest growing business in Canada, and this government is set on a course to destroy it.
Since 1984, the size and capabilities of the federal Department of Tourism have been steadily reduced by 75 per cent. The cuts to VIA Rail will effectively keep people from visiting many parts of this country. This all comes at a time when support for the industry should be
increasing in order to accommodate the world-wide rapid growth of tourism.
But most devastating of all is the proposed goods and services tax with its ill-conceived rebate which will be an absolute nuisance to travellers.
We have heard nothing but complaints from tour operators over this tax. As a result of an across-the-board 7 per cent sales tax on such items as hotel rooms, attractions and motor coach charters, many tour companies will no longer be able to market Canada as an affordable destination. A loss of tourist revenue translates into a loss of jobs.
I urge the government to stop this assault on the tourist industry by scrapping this tax and doing something for this country.

Madam Speaker, on Saturday, Canadians can vote for or against the goods and services tax in malls and public places throughout Canada. On Monday, they can vote at their workplace. I suspect they are going to vote against it; at least the opportunity is there.
But what about Parliament Hill? We in the NDP have set up a balloting station here on the Hill. To be specific, it will open on Monday at 10 a.m. in the Commonwealth Room right here in the Centre Block. We are inviting staff, visitors on the Hill and MPs to vote.
As a matter of fact, I would like to specifically invite the Tory MPs, the back-benchers, to come and vote on Monday at ten o'clock. It is a secret ballot. I know many of them would like to vote against the GST; here is an opportunity.

Madam Speaker, in today's Ottawa Citizen Liberal Senator Sidney Buckwold indicated that senators may likely delay the GST legislation.
Is the unelected Liberal senator saying that they will again attempt to block crucial government legislation for purely partisan purposes? I am sure that Senator Buckwold can recall his own words before a special joint committee on Senate reform. Senator Buckwold stated that the House of Commons is supreme. He also said: "Ultimately, in the case of a disagreement, the will of the House of Commons would prevail".
I hope the senator and his Liberal colleagues come to their senses and not only pass the GST legislation expeditiously but also pass C-21 so that Canadians can soon have the benefits of the law that that will bring.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a serious matter dealing with Senate reform. Last night the Prime Minister dealt another blow to Senate reform in the country when he said that he could not possibly accept an elected senator from the province of Alberta.
In a weird rearrangement of Canadian logic, he said he was elected by millions of people, the senator was only elected by thousands and that until he saw a new process in place completely, he would not accept an elected senator.
I would like the Prime Minister to use the House to explain to us how Meech Lake precludes an elected senator from Alberta. By denying Albertans the right to have another member in the Senate, he slows down the constitutional process and becomes the No 1 Dr. of Canadian politics.
April 6, 1990

Mr. Speaker, next week members will be voting on Bill C-62, the goods and services tax. Close to 80 per cent of Canadians across the country oppose this tax, but the government has chosen not to listen to the people. Canadians rightly believe that this tax, if passed, will result in higher taxes, higher inflation, higher interest rates, and higher unemployment.
The main supporters of this tax are big business, the income taxes of which are being reduced. The government has used closure at the committee stage and now for final reading of this bill in the Elouse of Commons. I suggest that it is doing so at its own peril.
We are urging Canadians across the country to phone their Conservative members of Parliament to tell them to vote against this bill. For example, constituents of Simcoe Centre told me Tuesday that their member said publicly that she does not listen to her constituents on the GST because they do not know what they are talking about.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
All across the country we have seen an unprecedented level of opposition to the government's goods and services tax. The ranks of discontent are growing from one end of the country to another. We see growing discontent in the Conservative ranks, in the Conservative caucus.
The more the government tries to explain this tax, the less Canadians like it. Eighty per cent of Canadians are now opposing the government's goods and services tax. If more and more Canadians are so fundamentally opposed to this tax, does this not mean there is something fundamentally wrong with it?
Oral Questions
Why will the Prime Minister not listen to Canadians and withdraw this tax now rather than try to force it through the House and shut off debate?

Mr. Speaker, we were elected by the people of Canada to lead and not to follow. We are going to lead even though the subjects are difficult and even though it means the government accepting a substantial degree of unpopularity, because doing what is right for the nation oftentimes means doing things that are difficult and unpopular.
Since 1924 there have been five Royal commissions or task forces telling the Parliament of Canada to get rid of the pernicious manufacturers' sales tax which we presently have. There was all-party agreement that the manufacturers' sales tax had to go. We agreed to get rid of it. The Liberals and NDP changed their minds because they are followers and not leaders.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government was elected to do what is right, but why does the Prime Minister not understand that what is right certainly depends not just on his personal judgment and that of his caucus but on that of Canadians? And, 80 per cent say what he wants to do is not right
Canadians are also saying that they do not believe the Prime Minister and his government when they say that the goods and services tax will not have much effect on inflation. Canadians know that when all of a sudden they start paying more tax on more things than ever before, they have less money in their pockets.
It is not surprising that workers in this country are taking steps now to protect themselves against the inflation this tax will bring and to protect themselves against the loss of purchasing power this goods and services tax will bring.
Why will the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance not admit today that this tax will cause more harm to the economy, more inflation, more damage than they have so far been willing to admit, and withdraw this tax? They should listen to Canadians when they say: "This tax is not right and we want the government to do what we have in mind on this essential subject".

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party challenged the Minister of Finance to a debate on this matter in Edmonton. The Minister of Finance went out and took on the finance

Oral Questions
critic from the Liberal Party, and we have not seen him in the House since.
Oh, oh!
Cheap, cheap. That's a lie.
Lie.
Lie.

The fact of the matter is that when challenged the Liberal Party said that what it was going give was more of the same: a manufacturers' sales tax that imposes a 13.5 per cent unfair burden on the backs of Canadian producers and that subsidizes imports so that importers can steal Canadian jobs.
We are making difficult and important but beneficial structural changes in the economy. We know that while it is unpopular today, it is in the national interest and, when given the choice during an election campaign between a party that took the tough decisions and a party that chose to hide its head in the sand, Canadians will vote for the Conservative Party.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the quality of what the Prime Minister is saying is demonstrated by the gross inaccuracy of his statement that the finance critic for the Liberal Party has not been in the House since the debate with the Minister of Finance in Edmonton. That is simply not true. The finance critic has been here continuously asking questions of the government on the goods and services tax, which the government has been unwilling to answer.

So I want to ask the Prime Minister: If his GST is so good for our economy and the present sales tax is so damaging, why did his government raise the present sales tax four times? Why, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition surprises me. For almost 50 years, five royal commissions or rather, parliamentary task forces have advised Parliament to get rid of the pernicious tax we have today and replace it with a tax on consumption.
You raised the tax four times.

The hon. member has been sitting in Parliament for a quarter of a century. He knows perfectly well that everyone agrees the existing tax is pernicious and damaging to the economy, both our national economy and that of Quebec or Alberta. We received unanimous recommendations from the various political groups in this House. The government, well aware that such action is not popular, then proceeded to get rid of a pernicious tax that is damaging to Canada's economy. We took this unpopular action, and lo and behold, the opposition changed its mind. Instead of supporting the government in a major initiative that will promote economic development in this country and create jobs for our young people, the Leader of the Opposition has taken his party back to the past instead of leading it to the future. Canadians, however, will vote for a government that faces the future, a new future for our young people.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
Letters from 29 grade four students, co-signed by their parents and with a covering letter from their teacher, Mrs. Donna Cohen of Elwick Community School, reached my constituency office this week. All fear that tax on books will make their education suffer. They have asked me to tell the Prime Minister: "Don't tax reading. Have a heart and listen."
Will the Prime Minister listen to the plea of these school children and accede to remove the GST on books? Would he listen, as well, to the sentiments of their parents expressed eloquently by one of them, Mrs. Poitras, who said: "Illiteracy is slowly becoming a problem of the past, don't make it a problem of the future"?

Mr. Speaker, to follow up on what the Prime Minister was saying, we have chosen a modem method of taxation which is very good for the country and which has been chosen by 48 other countries.
We have organized it in such a way that it will be fair to lower income people. We need to proceed on a very wide base and then give credits to lower income people so that they can make their choices. A family with an income
April 6, 1990

below $30,000 will be better off after reform than it was before.
This is a modern reform. It will help the economy, and it will continue our effort to extricate Canada from the awful situation the Liberal Party left us in, in 1984.

Mr. Speaker, if those school children and their parents were here, it would be very simple for them to tell the minister that he did not answer their plea; he did not answer their question.
My supplementary question is for the same minister. Perhaps this one will be answered directly and correctly.
Treatment of depression and behaviour disorders is lengthy and costly. Under the proposed GST psychoanalysts who are not physicians will have to tax their patients for the same treatment provided tax-free by psychoanalysts who are physicians.
Will the minister rectify this inequity by exempting all health care professionals from taxing their patients under the GST or, better still, by scrapping the GST altogether?

Mr. Speaker, we are not going to scrap the GST because it is a necessary, good and modem way of dealing with a problem.
Referring to his particular area of concern, we do not want to use the tax system to change the organization of life in Canada. At the present time, the provinces have a responsibility to determine which services are accepted under health care. We have decided that whenever two provinces make a decision that a particular service is covered, we will do the same.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State. Fifteen women demonstrating in the corridor outside the twelfth floor door of the Secretary of State's Vancouver office yesterday were dragged away and are to be charged with assault by trespass.
Oral Questions
Women across this country are being forced to risk criminal charges and conviction to let this minister know how devastating his cuts to women's centres are.
Will the minister meet with representatives of women's centres about the cuts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer clearly is yes. I have met with representatives of women's centres; I will meet with them; and I will want to continue to meet with them.
As far as the specifics of any incident are concerned, we understand that there are a lot of documents kept in the offices of the Secretary of State. The confidentiality of our clients is at risk. We must consider the security of our staff, who have provided excellent service to their clients through the years, and the client groups recognize how well they have been served.
Indeed, in this period some of them have been intimidated, hassled and harassed, not necessarily by the women themselves, but that is part of what has been taking place.
The administration has determined that we should be able to continue to operate and serve our clients well with some kind of security. I am not in charge of the security but the Undersecretary of State will continue to look after that and, I am sure, monitor it very carefully.

Mr. Speaker, does the minister not feel that dragging 15 women away from a locked door with people behind it is not intimidating, is not fear invoking and is not much of a response when one asks whether and when the minister will meet with women?
He says he has met with representatives of women's centres. He has never met with a representative of a women's centre in British Columbia. I would like to know where he met with women.
I would also like to know when he will respond to the letter from the hon. member for New Westminster- Burnaby about whether he will meet with the women MPs of the New Democratic Party, or are we too intimidating?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been willing to meet with as many of

April 6, 1990
Oral Questions
the groups that we serve as is possible. I am always interested in maintaining an open dialogue.
I have indicated quite clearly that all Canadians recognize how important a function women's centres fulfil and how essential it is that they continue to provide the opportunity for women to gain full equality in our society.
We have made progress, and maybe this is an important day to take the opportunity to examine what progress has actually been made. This government has a significant record of achievement. The appointments of women we have made to agency, boards and commission have more than doubled. The number of women at the deputy minister level has risen from seven in the 1984-85 period to more than twenty-one today.
Never again will women's programs or the activities of women be trivialized as they were in the days when the group opposite ran the government.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the hon. minister was not able to tell New Democratic women MPs when he would meet with us. However, we will see how many women in Canada are convicted under this government.
My third question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Yesterday, the Minister of Finance gave his assurance to my leader that should any province decide to penalize those on social assistance by deducting money from welfare benefits to compensate for their receipt of the GST rebate, he knew that all members of this House would roundly criticize that approach.
We have information, Mr. Minister of Health and Welfare, and I would like you to confirm this, that the government of Quebec is currently deducting $3 per adult per month, $5 for each of the first two children and $1 for each subsequent child from benefits given to social assistance recipients from federal sales tax credits and child tax credits. Would the minister please advise this House what he intends to do about it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when benefits are paid by the federal government to welfare recipients, we have a concern if provinces do not allow those benefits to be
passed on. In cases where this occurs, we attempt to encourage the province to reconsider its policy to ensure that the full benefit goes to those people who are intended to receive it from the federal government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State. Yesterday, his department announced funding for the Second Storey Women's Centre in Bridgewater from his department's project funding.
Can the minister assure the women of Canada that every group who lost core funding will receive comparable funds from Secretary of State's project funding and, more important, that women's groups are not being forced to compete with each other for ever decreasing funds.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have indicated very clearly, both in the House and outside, that there is increased program funding available. I have indicated that the program criteria have been opened up very carefully so that expenses which were previously admissible, under what some considered core funding-and hopefully I have helped everyone understand what that means-are now admissible under the project or program funding.
In order for the money to flow, in order for us to be able to help the women's centres continue to carry on their very vital activity, they must complete the applications. The applications must be sent in and then be approved and cheques will flow as they did to South Shore, where the Bridgewater Second Storey Women's Centre probably has its money this afternoon, with only a two-day delay from the time we received the application.

I only wish that the hon. the Secretary of State had had the benefit of attending the "wiener roast" that the women of Halifax held last Monday.

My supplementary question is also for the Secretary of State. The minister told us that women's groups now receive project funding. Can he explain why women who were demonstrating very peacefully at the Secretary of State's office in British Columbia were arrested yesterday?
April 6, 1990

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I greatly appreciate the hon. member's willingness to participate in projects to support women's centres. I think it is important that all Canadians do their part. Not all women's centres are supported by the government.
What about the group of B.C. women that were arrested yesterday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour. The minister knows that the people of southwestern Montreal are eagerly waiting for the government's response to the recommendations of the southwestern Montreal employment and economic recovery committee (CREESOM). In February, the minister promised that the government would respond by the end of March. Can he tell us today how the government intends to support the initiatives of the local community?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Corbeil (Minister of Labour and Minister of State (TVansports)):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount should know that for 20 years, his party let the economy of Montreal deteriorate to such an extent that the number of jobs in the Montreal area continually declined while his party was in power. Our government has only been in power for five years, but employment in Montreal has increased considerably and, as we have shown in the past, we are aware that some regions of the Island of Montreal need additional help to make up for what was not done during those 20 years.
When we got requests for help from the east end of Montreal, we responded to the satisfaction of those concerned, except that we would like to do even more to assist those who cannot enter the labour market now because they lack the necessary preparation and need
Oral Questions
training. So would he kindly tell his colleagues in the other place to pass Bill C-21 as quickly as possible?

Mr. Speaker, the minister did not answer the question. He knows people have now been waiting since November for the government's reply. In February, he told us we might get an answer by the end of March. Could he perhaps tell us today when the people of Southwest Montreal will receive the government's response to the CREESOM Committee's report on economic recovery and employment in Southwest Montreal? When will we have a reply from the government and the minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Corbeil (Minister of Labour and Minister of State (Transports)):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for reasons I mentioned earlier, we are giving very serious and careful consideration to our response to the CREESOM report, a response that will be aimed at correcting the same inequities the hon. member's party allowed to develop on the Island of Montreal for 20 years. An important aspect of our response to the CREESOM report concerns the issue of worker retraining and adjustment, and we waited as long as we could, in the hope the Liberal Party would change its mind. Considering the harm being done to people who are now unemployed and are waiting for retraining, we thought the Liberal Party would be able to persuade their colleagues in the other place to pass Bill C-21, so that we could provide the best possible response to the demands of Southwest Montreal. However, since that does not seem to be in the cards, we will have to give the right response just the same, in the next few weeks. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the members of CREESOM will be very pleased with our response.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance.
The economic policies of this Conservative government are having their desired effect. We have seen impossibly high interest rates, cuts in regional economic incentives, cuts in transfer payments for health and post-secondary education, cuts to UI and now we are seeing cuts in equalization payments to four provinces. For example, Prince Edward Island is going to lose $18 million, more dollars than they have lost already through Tory budgetary measures which will put P.E.I. into a

April 6, 1990
Oral Questions
deficit position because of this reduction in equalization payments. That province's finance minister has said it shows the direction the federal government is going, the provinces are being squeezed.
When is this government going to stand up for the poorer regions of this country?

Mr. Speaker, the record of this government stands for what we think about poorer regions of Canada. I will tell the hon. member that the results are what it is all about. This morning, the unemployment statistics are the lowest they have been since 1981.
Hear, hear!

How is that for devastation?
Of course, a lot remains to be done and this is what we are proposing to this House by modernizing our fiscal system, modernizing our trade with the free trade agreement, organizing our economy so that the full force and capacity can be there to serve Canadians. The government has a major role to play and is playing it and I am very proud of our decisions, particularly concerning the lower income regions of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the unemployed and the people in the fishery in Newfoundland do not quite agree with what the minister is saying. They and the farmers in Saskatchewan, women, women's groups, native Canadians and the poor are all feeling the cuts in their pocketbooks, and their families are feeling the cuts, too.
How do you have the nerve to tell Canadians families-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I ask the hon. member to put his question.

I ask
the minister, how could this government possibly have the nerve to tell Canadian families, who cannot make ends meet, that they will be better off with less? How can less be more?

Mr. Speaker, the responsibility of this government is to ensure that the services the government has to provide to the population are there. The best way to do that is to get our fiscal house and economy in order. There are no short cuts.
I remind the hon. member that in our last budget we were very careful to devise our transfer payments in a way that would protect the poorer regions of Canada. But yet again, we must all tackle the deficit and debt together.
The government has maintained its increased programs at 3.5 per cent over the last five years, while the provinces have been moving up to 7 per cent, 8 per cent, 9 per cent, and in certain instances to 14 per cent. This cannot go on forever. This is money we are taking from Canadians. We have made transfer payments in a way that eastern provinces in particular and lower income people will be better served by our transfer programs.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of State for Finance. At the same time, I would like to offer him my unswerving support for what must be done, namely, the implementation of the goods and services tax.
I realize that in the past the Department of Finance has done a remarkable job in its economic projections, and there is no good reason to believe that this will change.
However, I would like to know the government reaction in the event that the goods and services tax should take in more revenue than is anticipated. I know that the people of Regina would reject these funds being used to increase government spending, therefore I would like to ask the minister to tell us and the people of Regina- Wascana that if extra revenue should occur, will it be put to further reducing our deficit or will it be used for increased program expenditures?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the hon. member that the government has always said that the GST is an integral part of deficit reduction.
April 6, 1990

As far as managing the pressures within the system is concerned, we have reserves that are there for that purpose. To the extent that we receive greater income or greater revenues than expected from the GST or from any other source, of course they will be applied to deficit reduction.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and it concerns the disturbing news that the federal government is again transferring its deficit on to the backs of the poorest of the provinces.
In the P.E.I. legislature yesterday-and my hon. colleague just alluded to it-the provincial Minister of Finance, Gilbert Clements, indicated that, because of an unannounced change in the equalization formula, Ottawa will save over $1 billion in 1989 which he says will mean big revenue losses for all of Atlantic Canada.
Will the Prime Minister confirm that there has been a change in the equalization formula, and will he kindly tell us why these changes were kept hidden from the provincial finance ministers until last Friday?

Mr. Speaker, I have not had the pleasure of reading the statement by the Treasurer of Prince Edward Island, to which my hon. friend referred, but I can tell him that the budget of the province of Prince Edward Island appears to be in virtual balance. It is a balanced budget in large measure due to the massive transfers of federal funds from Ottawa to Prince Edward Island.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the Prime Minister that that budget surplus has now been turned into a budget deficit in Prince Edward Island because of the $1 billion in cuts that it found out about last Friday. I will send the Right Hon. Prime Minister a copy of the statement so that he can read it.
My supplementary question is for the Prime Minister. At the veiy time that the Atlantic economy has been battered by a collapsing fishery, by hundreds of millions of dollars in cuts to federal EPFs, and withdrawal by the
Oral Questions
federal government of regional development programs, we now find out there could be up to $1 billion cut in equalization payments to the poorest of provinces.
What actions does the Prime Minister plan to take to address this very serious loss of revenue to all of Atlantic Canada, and why does he continue to adopt and practice the cruel "kick them when they're down game" on the Atlantic provinces of this country?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend knows full well that he is doing and has been doing a very serious disservice to the facts.
His partisanship obscures any value that he may bring to the House of Commons. Get the chip off your shoulder, and people will start listening to you.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

This government, Mr. Speaker, is in the process of bringing forward a program for the Atlantic fishery, which has increased transfer payments to Atlantic Canada, increased EPF payments to Atlantic Canada and increased regional development programs from $182 million, where they were when the hon. member's party was in office, to $400 million a year. Premier Frank McKenna described this government in terms of ACOA as having brought forward the single most important vehicle for regional development in the history of Atlantic Canada.
My hon. friend should be congratulating this government for what it has done for Atlantic Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State (Finance).
A minute or two ago, I heard him say that the goods and services tax has always been intended to be an integral part of deficit reduction. Yet we heard the Minister of Finance say in this House that the goods and services tax would be revenue neutral, which to most people would mean that the tax would not bring in any more revenue than the existing manufacturers' sales tax.

April 6, 1990
Oral Questions
How can the tax be at one and the same time revenue neutral and be an integral part of deficit reduction? No wonder Canadians don't believe anything the government says about the goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that the hon. Leader of the Opposition suffers from an acute case of selective listening.
He should have listened to my colleague, the Minister of Finance, when he indicated that GST would reduce the deficit, because the present pillar of the federal sales tax is a porous one. That means that as it grows, companies evade tax. There is a lot of tax evasion and it threatens our resources. In putting together a modem, efficient system of sales tax the GST will prevent this and ensure that the government can deliver its programs and pay for them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State (Finance) says that the present manufacturers' sales tax is a porous pillar.
Canadians would like to know, if that is the case, why has the government raised this tax not one, not two, not three, but four times since it came into office, and the revenue, since it came into office, has grown by billions of dollars to the present level of over $18 billion? If that tax is so flawed, why has it done this?
I ask the minister, how can Canadians believe anything that the government says, when he says the new tax will be an integral part of deficit reduction and the Minister of Finance says the same tax will be revenue neutral? It is simply not believable.

Mr. Speaker, you have to run with your old car until you buy a new one so we have made use of a system which was not a good system. We have devised a way of changing it. We have a system where there are 22,000 different private arrangements with companies, so this is a terrible system. It is an old system which has been there for 64 years.
We announced our colour before the election. We introduced a White Paper, we introduced a technical paper and we introduced a bill. Meanwhile, we have had to make do with a bad tax.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Last December, the Minister of National Revenue threatened the Canada Council over its funding of the Buddies in Bad Times Theatre Company in Toronto. This week, the chair of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture threatened the National Galleiy with a funding cut because the gallery bought a painting "Voice of Fire" which was a controversial buy.
Does the Prime Minister's government still believe in the arm's length principle of our cultural agencies, a principle that means that while the government funds the agencies, the government does not get involved in the operation of the agencies? Does the government still believe in that principle, and if it does, will it start acting like it?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, we believe very strongly in the concept of the arm's length arrangement with these funding agencies, although I suppose, like all Canadians, voters in Charlevoix, for example, are sometimes astonished when they see a grant for say $12,000 go out for something the rough equivalent of studying the sex life of the eastern fly. They find it difficult to understand the value of that for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is again talking out of both sides of his mouth. Either he believes in the principle or he doesn't.
It is easy to take a cheap shot at the National Gallery, as the chair of the cultural committee has, but he did not have the guts to show up when John Kim Bell came before our committee on native matters.
Given what the chair of that committee has done in the past with respect to the advertisements on the CBC, the trips to Africa for hunting, the comments on the galleiy now, will the government act like it believes in the arm's length principle and replace the chair of that committee?

Mr. Speaker, I am astonished at my friend's question because this government has increased the discretionary spend-
April 6, 1990

mg limits for the groups that dispense funds at an arm's length relationship with the government.
There is no case on record that I am aware of-and I would be happy if my hon. friend could bring one forward-of the intervention of myself or any member of the government attempting to insinuate himself or herself into the decision-making process of one of these granting agencies. Our attitude is best described by the fact that we have increased the funding to these agencies. We fully respect and acknowledge the importance of the arm's length relationship.
We also hope that those who make the decisions in granting these funds realize that they are not functioning in a vacuum. They are functioning in Canada in given circumstances. We hope that they will apply their best judgment, with an understanding that they are dealing with hard earned taxpayers' money.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Public Works. It seems to me that the government is spending a great deal of time these days in court defending the tendering process for the GST data centre.
Can the minister tell the House whether the government went into this process with the decision having already been made?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. We did this transaction in the usual way. A decision to lease was made by the accommodations branch and then it went to the realty branch. It was a process that was done to the best of our ability in an open and honest way.
When it was questioned we paid attention to Mr. Justice Strayer's decision. We carried out a re-evaluation and we decided it would be in everyone's best interest if we, despite the pressures of time, opened the tendering process again. This has now been done. The bids are being evaluated. The deputy minister will bring a recommendation forward and we hope that this will be done next week.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, does the minister agree that by changing the rules in the course of the process, his government has created a certain amount of chaos for people tendering bids for the data centre? Will the government investigate charges that the selection process is unfair and subjective?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would reject immediately any suggestion that the selection process was falsified. As far as changing the specifications is concerned, we did not change the specifications, we only attempted to reflect as much as possible the special requirements that our client department, namely Revenue Canada, required such as security, access, working conditions and important things like this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister for External Relations. At a time when the government has cut $666 million from the budget for the Canadian International Development Agency, spread over a period of three years, how can it justify spending $600,000 on the office of our ambassador-at-large and personal representative of the Prime Minister, the Hon. George Hees, who is acting as an advisor on food distribution in Third World countries?

Mr. Speaker, I was away from the House and I read with dismay and astonishment that a question had been raised that would in any way tarnish the reputation of one of Canada's outstanding war heroes and parliamentarians, the Hon. George Hees.
This Parliament and this country should consider itself fortunate to have someone like George Hees undertake sensitive, important responsibilities checking on the distribution of food world-wide. I can tell you that at 75 years of age and after a lifetime of service to Canada, both in times of war and in peace, I was honoured to be

April 6, 1990
Oral Questions
able to appoint George Hees to that position. He has come through and filled that job in an excellent fashion which brings great honour to every member of the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish the Prime Minister had listened to my question because I was extremely careful. I respect Mr. Hees, and every member of this Parliament, I am sure, respects the outstanding record that he has contributed to this country.
But the fact remains, does the Minister for External Relations not feel that given this government's commitment to thrift, which it talks about so consistently across this country, that this office, costing $600,000, represents at least a duplication and at worst, a triplication, of the supervisory role in food distribution in the Third World and that this money might be better spent on the food itself and the aid to these foreign countries.

Mr. Speaker, the insinuation in that question, and I know my hon. friend does not intend it that way, is very unfortunate and very misleading. There have been no additional costs to the Government of Canada, apart from the ongoing salary for the hon. George Hees.
And his staff, and his flights.

My hon. friend has staff himself to help him do his job. Would he suggest that Mr. Hees, doing a sensitive international job for the Government of Canada, not receive some modest assistance himself?
Surely it is appropriate that if you ask someone, a minister of the Crown, a member of Parliament for 35 years and one of Canada's most distinguished public servants, to undertake a sensitive job to make sure that food is distributed properly to Third World countries in the most efficient and expeditious manner possible you would want him to have the services of a modest degree of support staff.
I can tell my hon. friend that I was delighted to appoint Mr. Hees. I was also delighted to appoint the hon. Ed Broadbent to a job. I can tell you that the support staff that Mr. Broadbent enjoys, as well as the general salary and benefits package is a very nice one and compares favourably with that of other senior public servants. Why would it be otherwise? Mr. Broadbent is serving his country well. Mr. Hees is serving his country well. Why
would you pick on someone like George Hees? Why not just acknowledge the fact that he has been a tremendous public servant and let us stand up and celebrate what he has done for his country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Prime Minister if he feels it is appropriate at a time when budgets have been reduced for overseas development assistance that he have a personal envoy who reports directly to him? Is it not public information, this very crucial issue of food distribution?
Further to the question from my colleague from Kingston and the Islands, does the Prime Minister feel it is appropriate that this should be a triplication of work with CIDA, with non-governmental organizations and with Canadian missions overseas? Does he feel it is appropriate that $612,000 per year is allocated for his personal information?

Mr. Speaker, I am absolutely astonished at the fact that the NDP would allow a member of Parliament to raise this kind of question.
Budgets were being reduced but we still proceeded with the creation of the International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development, of which Ed Broadbent is the president, and I can tell you that the cost of running that institute is substantially higher than $600,000 a year. The fact that we are cutting budgets does not mean that we should not be concerned about Third World development or about human rights.
In the cases of both Mr. Broadbent and Mr. Hees, they are doing a tremendous service for Canada. The hon. member in raising these questions is trying-inadvertently I hope-to undermine the reputation of Mr. Hees and should apologize to Mr. Hees in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear that in no way do I impugn the reputation of Mr. Hees.
In light of this, will the Prime Minister now reassign Mr. Hees to a more appropriate act in his absolutely demonstrated commitment to the Veterans Independence Program? That is where the money should be
April 6, 1990

Routine Proceedings
going. If the Prime Minister is going to have a personal envoy have Mr. Hees work in the area in which he has expertise and demonstrated commitment.

Mr. Speaker, this question is apparently generated by cuts in budgets, if the hon. member wants the amount of $600,000. cut out, I can tell her that the cost of operating Mr. Broadbent's new institute is in the neighbourhood of $3 million. Would she want that cut? I do not think it should be cut, because even though we are going through difficult times, human rights is vital. Mr. Broadbent is a very good person to defend the cause of human rights just as George Hees is an outstanding person to undertake the responsibilities he is undertaking.
The NDP should be ashamed of themselves. This is a cheap shot.

Mr. Speaker, earlier during Question Period I may have violated a rule of the House when I referred to the absence of a member, which I ought not to have done. I think it is a generally accepted rule of the House that we not refer to each other's absences.
