Madam Speaker, I have two petitions to present today pursuant to Standing Order 31.
I am pleased to present the first one signed by 55 Nepean petitioners who are asking the Government of Canada to intervene in the release of one of Canada's citizens, Mr. Yih-Sheh Leo, who is being held in prison in Taiwan as a result of political interference for exercising his freedom of speech.

Madam Speaker, the second petition relates to the goods and services tax. This petition is signed by several Nepean petitioners. It is something that is ongoing in Nepean and the people of my riding are very concerned about the imposition of this unfair tax.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition with respect to government cuts to the budget for women's centres. It is signed by approximately 500 people from central Vancouver Island.
I would like to point out that one of the signatories of this petition is Caroline Gran, the minister responsible for the status of women in the province of British Columbia.

Madam Speaker, I have three petitions to present to the House today.
The first petition was collected in the city of Halifax. It is a petition directed at Parliament and concerns the intention of Canada Post to close the Halifax shopping centre corporate outlet at the end of March. The petitioners suggest that this is a major disruption and inconvenience to the large number of senior citizens, families, and other individuals in the neighbourhood who depend on the products and services, and inconveniences others who use one of the largest shopping centres in Nova Scotia.
April 6, 1990

The petitioners call on Parliament to ensure that Canada Post reverses its short-sighted plans and keeps a full service Canada Post operation at the Halifax shopping Centre.
This petition is signed by 750 people and is the first of two petitions I have submitted for certification by the House.
The second petition is signed by 165 residents of the Saskatchewan communities of Watson, Englefield, Quill Lake, but primarily from Watson, Saskatchewan.
They call on Parliament to save the national postal system and to ask Canada Post to stop its ill-conceived plans to sell off the postal service to big business. They say that rural post offices not only provide the service they need, but offer an important federal presence in their community.
The petitioners call on Parliament to refrain from putting retail postal outlets where there are existing post offices in their communities. The petitioners did not ask for retail postal outlets, they do not need them, and they do not want them.

The
third and final petition is signed by a number of residents from the province of British Columbia. It concerns the goods and services tax.
The petitioners note that the proposed goods and services tax is an unfair form of taxation because of its lack of regard for taxpayers' ability to pay. They call upon Parliament to reject the current bill on the goods and services tax and replace it with a reformed tax system that would provide for fairer taxes on Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I have two petitions to present today on behalf of the residents of Metropolitan Toronto and region in support of Mr. Yih-Sheh Leo.
They urge the Canadian government to take immediate and effective measures to secure his release from the Taiwan government where he is being held prisoner.
Routine Proceedings

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition on behalf of people in my riding who ask the government to reject the GST bill.

I have two more petitions on the same subject from Canadians from Baie Comeau to just about every small city between there and St. Laurent.
The imposition of the new goods and services tax will cause serious and unfair hardship to low and middle income Canadians and they ask this government to reject the project.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to table in the House a number of petitions signed by Quebecers from Plessisville, Laurierville, Princeville, Victoriaville, Art-habaska and Sainte-Rosalie, who are vehemently opposed to the position taken by this government in wishing to impose a new tax on goods and services.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition certified according to Standing Order 36 from a number of people opposed to the goods and services tax because it is unfair and bears more heavily on low income Canadians than high income Canadians.
They therefore urge Parliament to reject the goods and services tax and to cause the government to shift the tax burden from ordinary Canadians to those who are able to pay.
I have a further petition signed by 200 Canadians from various provinces, much more specifically concerned with the fact that since Confederation there has been a zero rate of tax on magazines, books and newspapers, and the government now proposes to include them in the goods and services tax, although uninhibited dissemination of the printed word as a cornerstone of democracy, culture, education, and a literate and productive society will be negatively affected by that application.

April 6, 1990
Routine Proceedings
Therefore they call upon Parliament to reaffirm the historic principles embodied in the tax-free status for the printed word by retaining the zero rate in the GST legislation and regulations.

I have two more petitions, Madam Speaker. One is from a number of residents of Toronto who urge this Parliament to join with the Assembly of First Nations and the Innu of Labrador and other aboriginal peoples of northern Canada in opposing the use of their lands for NATO-NORAD attack training.
They demand that Canada withdraw its application for a NATO-NORAD base there and redirect Canada's NATO-NORAD funding toward enabling Canada's aboriginal peoples to regain control of their lands and their livelihood and promoting sustainable development for all Canadians.

Therefore they humbly pray and call upon Parliament to maintain, improve and modernize VIA Rail service in those areas of the country where it can provide a more rapid, economical, safe, convenient, environmentally sound and energy efficient alternative to other means of transportation.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am devastated that we have to speak on this issue yet again in the House.
We are looking at the Secretary of State cut of $23 million in total. We are looking specifically at the cut to women's programs of $1.6 million. We are also looking at the difference between core funding and project funding.
The hon. minister told us this morning that some women did not understand the difference, and I assure you that women understand all too well the difference between core funding and project funding.
First, the number of programs affected by cuts in core funding is 76, and I will discuss those programs further along in my remarks.
Second, core funding is a long-term kind of funding. It allows for long-term planning and for autonomy, an arm's length relationship to government policy. Project funding, on the other hand, is short term and limited to a particular purpose. If the government is changing the rules vis-a-vis the titles of these funding programs, all that is happening is something similar to a geometry

*

^I
April 6, 1990

program in high school: it is changing the letters on the theorems.
What is really happening for women across Canada is that they are being forced into competition with each other because the dollars are less. We have a $23 million cut right across the board in the Secretary of State and a $1.6 million in core funding, but the real answer is that there is less money available.
To be told as we have been told over and over again, today, yesterday, and so on, that women's centres will receive their project funding if they apply is insufficient and not at all reassuring. The women's centres that face these cuts nation-wide include 40 women's centres in Quebec, 7 in Newfoundland and in excess of 30 in the province of British Columbia. These women's centres provide a range of services that is unique and will not be offered elsewhere to Canadian women.
I recall when these women's centres first began to be set up in Canada. We have again been admonished by a number of people on the government side of the Elouse to look elsewhere for funding. I doubt that there is a woman sitting in this House today who does not know the exigencies of fund raising for women's groups and organizations that support women's projects.
Whether we are talking about national groups like the YWCA, or whether we are talking about individual women's centres, the problem is the same: without core funding from the government it becomes a futile task of going back to the same people time and again for ever decreasing dollars.
If the government is committed to equality for women, if the government is committed to alleviating the very real sufferings that gender inequity creates in this country, then core funding is the only answer.
Look at the things that this government decided to fund when it cut a paltry $1.6 million and devastated women's centres across this country.
We have just sat through the presenting of petitions in this House. We heard of thousands more Canadians who are against the GST. Yet, this government in its effort to sell this possibly most unpopular program in the history of Canadian parliamentary democracy has allocated between $11 million and $14 million, to sell the GST: $1.6 million to devastate women's programs nation-wide

and $14 million to convince Canadians to swallow a pill that they absolutely do not want.
In my riding of Halifax visiting cabinet ministers will now have an office. This office will be decorated at a cost of $1.6 million. The same amount of money, $1.6 million, so that visiting cabinet ministers can have a place to relax in the city of Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext: So they will have a place to work.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
Well work, relax. I assure the hon. Minister of Justice that she can use my office whenever she wants if she needs a place to work. I would be happy to let her have it.
I suggest to the minister that my colleague from Dartmouth and her colleague from Halifax West would be happy to let her use their offices on the rare occasions when cabinet ministers need to work in Halifax.
Madam Speaker, $1.6 million for an office in one of the provincial capitals. The women of Canada understand what core funding is; they understand what project funding is; but they do not understand why they lost $1.6 million and why the exact amount is given to decorate an office.
Ceremonial state activities were allocated a $3 million increase in this most recent budget. I agree that there is a need for Canadians to see and to celebrate their country. But when women and children are suffering across the country, that is a $3 million allocation vis-avis a $1.6 million cut.
Finally, this year the Canadian Security Intelligence Service was allocated a $32.6 million increase. I am not necessarily saying that CSIS does not do a valuable job. That remains to be seen. The jury is out. But could we not have given CSIS $31 million and left $1.6 million for women's centres across the country? I think, in view of what this cut will mean to women on a national level, from St. John's to Victoria, that might have been something that could have been included in the budget.
Core funding no longer exists, we are told. But project funding has been increased. Project funding does not give the women's centres the kind of continuity and security they need. In spite of the protestations from the other side, it does not necessarily pay the rent. It does

April 6, 1990
Supply
not necessarily pay the salaries for co-ordinators, and it does not necessarily pay the heat, lights and other things necessary to set up an office.
It is crucially important that it be brought to the attention of all members of this House, the kinds of things these women's centres do. We were told earlier that the federal government is not supposed to provide services for victims of sexual assault or battered wives, and so on. But one of the absolutely crucial services performed by women's centres is that they are a clearing house and a communications network for women who are otherwise alienated and isolated from the help they have to have.
Surely, no one needs to stand in the House yet again and remind any of us of the incidence of abuse of women and children. It is at a shocking and unacceptable level. Women's centres are in the front lines of fighting this abuse. They are not transition houses. They are not shelters. But frequently, for a woman in an extreme situation, the only place she knows to call is that place down on Main Street or that house where those women have those programs. She calls and is referred to the proper social service agency, if indeed there is one in the town in which she lives. If there is not a transition house or a particular agency, normally there are networks of women volunteers who will try to provide her with support and help to get her out of the untenable situation she is in.
Women across the country work an unbelievable number of hours as volunteers in women's centres. They work to help other women. They work, many of them, because there is no money available to pay them salaries, and so they do it out of a sense of survival for all women, out of a sense of duty, and out of a sense of what we must do to pull together.
The salaries that come from the core funding are hardly the kind of salaries to which anyone would aspire. The payment of part time and full time co-ordinators is still barely above a subsistence level in the country. Think about it again. We have talked about a maximum of 60 centres that are closing in the country, and the cut that is closing these centres is a mere $1.6 million. Start
dividing up that quotient and see what it means on an individual level.
One centre in Nova Scotia was receiving $46,000 and another $49,000. Well, nobody is living high on the hog on the portion of those grants that pay for salaries. Nobody is able to deliver services of the kind that were being referred to this morning.
These centres are clearing houses. They are places of communication. They are referral services. They are places of safety where women can walk in the door and say: "Tell me what to do next. Tell me who to go to for help. Tell me who can help me in this situation in which I find myself, that I can no longer deal with. Tell me". That is what women are saying in transition houses in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Quebec, and British Columbia.
Even if the project funding keeps the doors open a little while longer, without core funding the long term hard work of these centres will go for naught. The switch from core funding to project funding is the end for many of them and the beginning of the end for the rest.
The cuts to the Secretary of State women's program did not just affect women's centres. Funding to research organizations was also cut by 20 per cent, organizations such as the Canadian Council on Learning Opportunities for Women, the Canadian Research Institute on the Advancement of Women, the British Columbia Women's Research Centre, and in Quebec, Nouveau depart.
These are organizations that have done incredible service for women in the area of knowledge and communications. They are the women who know what problems are facing other women in the country, what resources are available for them, what educational facilities are there, and what research has been done to assist them in a myriad of activities as they emerge slowly into a world that is all too slowly heading toward the eventual goal of gender equality. Again, these organizations are run on shoestring budgets. Many women involved with these organizations do so on a voluntary basis.
One of the issues which relates to core funding and relates to the whole spectrum of the way the government deals with women is, of what value is the contribution of women? What is the value of the work that women do in women's centres, with CCLOW, with CRIAW, NAC, and
April 6, 1990

the various other organizations across the country? What is the value of that work? It appears that the answer is, not very high.
We saw the increases to various government agencies. What did we see across the board for women? Cuts and decreases. We did not see anything that would tell women there is a light at the end of the tunnel, that we want to help them, or that we want to show them that what they do is valuable. We want to see gender equality as an end in the country at least within the lifetimes of some of us sitting here in the House.
I know that there are individual members on the other side of the House committed to this. I know this. I have worked on committees with those members. I know how they feel and I know what they think. I know it must be difficult, but there has to be a political will.
Women make up 52 per cent of the population. While it is true that not all women support the kinds of things we are talking about here today, it is also true that the vast majority of women in the country do support these things. The vast majority of women look to the government and say: "Why are you undervaluing and undercutting what it is we have worked so hard for over the past 10 to 15 years? Why are you stifling the voice of women by cutting grants to research? Why are you undoing the work that for the last 15 to 20 years of the most recent exhibition of a woman's movement has developed?"
Every woman in the Chamber has some experience of that work, some more than others. Every one of us has had some experience in that area. We are all, to a smaller or larger degree, committed to this work and to the development of gender equality. At least, I thought we were.
The women of Canada have received too many blows from the government, particularly over the past several years. We see that abortion is going to be recriminalized in the country. We hear that women's groups across the country are crying for better medical services, better access to medical services, better education and training, more child care and more of the services that are not frills or frosting but the absolute essentials for a decent life.
We know that the feminization of poverty is a fact of life in our country. We know that when girl babies are
Supply
bom, as they go along in life they can expect, if they are university educated, to make as much money as a male high school graduate; if they are professionally educated, to make as much money as a single university degree graduate who is male.
My hon. colleague across the way shakes her head, but she can look at the statistics. Statistics Canada will tell her the truth.
These women can expect, no matter how much money they make or where they live, to have difficulty in finding adequate child care for any children they will have. They can expect to have difficulties and systemic barriers facing them in whatever profession or walk of life they choose. The vast majority of them can expect to end up in pink-collar ghettos. An unfortunate percentage of them can expect to be battered by their partners in life.
It is not good enough, Madam Speaker. You know it is not, I know it is not, and members on both sides of the House know it is not. The women's centres from St. John's to Victoria have been there and will continue somehow to be there. But the women who staff them will be paid less. There will be days in the winter that the centres will have to shut down because they will not be able to afford heat. There will be other times when they will not be there to provide essential services because they have lost core funding.
The women of Canada are fighting a battle that for a while we thought we might win. Without the political will, and without the dollars that that political will can and must generate, the women of Canada will lose this battle. They will lose this battle and we will all be the poorer for it. But they will not lose this battle quietly and they will not lose it without inflicting some wounds of their own.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to make an intervention at this time. Equality and social justice for women in Canada is a high priority for all of us in the House and all of us across Canada.
We can be very proud that just recently the first female Minister of Justice was appointed. We are delighted that we now have the first woman justice minister and we can be truly proud of the outstanding background which she brings to this portfolio.

April 6, 1990
Supply
Let us get to the core funding applications and project funding applications about which my colleague has spoken. The core funding applications have been annual applications, not long term applications. They must be applied for every year. Every project needs to have an application.
In the last few weeks the minister has reiterated the importance of flexibility in the program. These moneys are to be used for such things as rent, light and heat. The minister has asked the women's groups to forward applications. The staff has been available to assist in filling out the applications. We are prepared to expedite those applications in order that the funding is available. I think the hon. member, instead of inciting a situation, needs to see how we can work together to make this a very substantial program so we can attain what we are all looking for and that is equality and social justice for women.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her comments, but I am afraid I must correct a misconception on her part. It is difficult to understand the difference between core funding and project funding. It may have been a slip of the tongue, but what she said was that each project must be approved separately. That is quite true for project funding, but core funding is different.
Core funding is done usually every year, I agree. There are different lengths of time, but a year is the average. Core funding is considered to be renewable and it covers certain things that project funding does not. I further tell the hon. member, with the greatest of respect, that I asked the minister today in Question Period, whether or not he could assure the women of Canada that all those groups which lost their core funding would get comparable funding under project funding. I am afraid I received no such assurance and neither did the women of Canada.
Core funding pays for things like rent, heat, lights, and co-ordinator's salaries. Project funding relates to a specific project and, thus far, it is not within the project funding terms of reference-so far as we know and so far as we have been told by consultations today with the minister's department- whether or not a project can be keeping open the centre. It does not appear that can be the case, that you must have a specific project.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to make a comment and ask a question. I would like to comment on a comment, if I may.
The Conservative member across the way has just said that the government wants to see equality and social justice for women. Well, why not just restore the funding? Why not just admit it was a mistake, or it has gone wrong, or it is not working, and just restore the funding? That would be the simple way of doing it. Governments have done that in the past.
We had a provincial government in B.C. that I never voted for and never liked, but sometimes the old Premier, W.A.C. Bennett, would say: "Well, we're taking another look at it" and something would change when there was a public outcry. Why the gobbledegook about core funding and project funding? That is just putting poor women who are overworked and underpaid through more bureaucratic hassle. Just restore the funding.
I have a question for the hon. member from the Liberal Party who just spoke. Is there another agenda here from the government? She mentioned more money for propaganda and advertising the GST. There is more money for the secret police. Are we, in fact, seeing the government trying to punish what they think are political opponents in the women's movement or, for example, native people? The government cut back native communications programming and so on. It is a paranoid government that considers that somehow these groups are not on its team. They are not the big business boys so it is punishing them. They are the groups in society which can least afford to be punished.
I wonder if the hon. member is hinting that there is another agenda there on the government's part and that it is not just an oversight. Is it a real agenda to kill these kinds of groups and to put them down, perceived in the paranoid way of the government that somehow these groups are in opposition to what it stands for?

Madam Speaker, I would just like to pick up on my question before the member from the NDP spoke. It was in relation to the question posed by the hon. member for Halifax to the minister.
What we are encouraging the women and groups of women to do is to make application. We want to keep the women's centres open and to have those applications in order to be flexible so that we can keep the centres open and make it possible for those programs that have been set forth by the women's centres.
In the blanket question that the hon. member is asking, we want to look at each application. Our staff is ready to co-operate at any time in order to provide the service.
I just want to say to the hon. member that the social justice program for women is really quite a remarkable one. If you think of the women in positions of power, 30
Supply
per cent of the positions on all boards and commissions are now held by women, which is a remarkable increase from when her party was in power over some years.
We have the employment equity bill, the federal contracts program, the Canadian Jobs Strategy, and the changes to UI Act, Bill C-21, that we think is important to get through for training. There are the family violence centres and initiatives that have been put forth. There is $40 million in additional funds over the next four years to help the problem of family violence, $22 million for 500 new transition houses, and $18 million to help improve social and health services for Canadian women. Now that is a remarkable accomplishment.
When looking at the total picture, these are remarkable initiatives that the government has pursued and we will continue to work with the women of Canada in order to provide that social justice that we believe is so important.

speechtext:
I have just a short response, Madam Speaker. I thank the hon. member for Scarborough Centre. I cannot imagine why the women of Canada do not feel better. They just feel so good, it is a wonder then-heads do not fall off.
The number of programs can be cited and recited by the government members. There is this idea that the women just have to reapply. Why is the government changing the rules in midstream? Give them back the money, $1.6 million. The minister himself has said it is peanuts. So give them the peanuts and let the centres stay open. What is the matter? Are you afraid there is something going on in there that is going to do something dreadful to you? Come on. Be good. Be honest. Give those women back the money they need.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must certainly affirm what was just said by the member representing the Liberal party.
Before I get into my own remarks, I would like to extend my greetings or regrets to the member for Burnaby-New Westminster who was the instigator of this resolution and this debate today. I can tell you that this member, who has worked so hard for women, is at this time meeting with women's groups in British Colum-

April 6, 1990
Supply
bia and will soon be meeting with women's groups right in the front lines in other provinces as well.
We are extremely concerned about what the government is doing to women, particularly to women's centres. This is just the tip of the iceberg. It is really the symbol of so many things that are wrong about the government.
I would like to say, before I get to women's centres, that in my view the most cruel and inhumane cuts in this very devastating budget were cuts to Secretary of State funding. These cuts affected a number of groups: aboriginal groups, ethnic minorities as well as women. They were cuts also to the kind of programs that are helping powerless groups to speak out and to work for equality, cuts to advocacy groups of all kinds, to national groups in the case of native people who are working towards self-government, to communications publications that help groups to network and bring their issues before people to gain broad support, cuts to research and to self-help groups. I would call women's centres a selfhelp program.
Why has the government chosen to cut funding for disadvantaged groups that are struggling to achieve equality? I would just like to requote the statement of my colleague a few minutes ago. He questioned whether or not this was not the "actions of a paranoid government that is punishing political opponents"? I think this was a very astute comment by my colleague. Why are government members, and particularly the Minister responsible for the Status of Women and the Secretary of State himself, deliberately trying to silence the voice of native groups who are working towards self-government, ethnic minorities who are pressing to end racism and to achieve equal opportunities for various ethnic groups, women's organizations that are front-line advocates for equality which are part of the feminist movement across Canada and the feminist publications that are the link between women in this very large country of ours?
Obviously, the government does not want criticism. It does not want criticism of its policies. Of course, women in particular have had very much to say about this and about the fact that we are not moving nearly quickly enough towards equality in the country. My colleagues have noted a number of examples, as did the Liberal speaker a few minutes ago.
The government really does not want to have these groups that are speaking out for disadvantaged and so-called powerless people becoming powerful. That is, of course, what is needed. We need advocacy groups that will represent people across the country and get to the government, not only to criticize but to put forward positive ideas and positive programs and amendments to legislation and so on. I think this is an essential part of our democratic system. It is very important that the government continue to fund such groups. The government is deliberately cutting the voice of the most disadvantaged of Canadians.
We have heard over and over again today, and we just heard a few minutes ago from the member for Scarborough, about what a wonderful job the government has done in appointments. What good is lip service about equality, which it is also great at espousing, and token appointments to a few jobs, if, at the front lines in communities, women are getting poorer and they are increasingly being battered and abused? Their rights are not being respected. They are not able to get into equal employment with decent rates of pay, and they do not have child care. At the same time, the women's centres, which are there to help with critical problems, are being closed because of the need for a relatively small amount of money from the government which it has deliberately taken away from women.
This government also is the government that espouses multiculturalism. I say this as the multicultural critic. At the same time, it has cut federal funding for heritage languages, for advocacy groups that are speaking out at the federal level, and for citizenship and language training programs that are absolutely essential for newcomers to the country and others. These are all part of the same pattern.
Today, however, we want to concentrate particularly on the whole problem of the budget cuts of $1.6 million to women's centres.
Where is the minister who is responsible for the status of women? She has not been in the House today. She has not answered questions-

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
I think the record will show that the member who just spoke has been on her feet much more this week than the Minister responsible for the Status of Women.
However, let us get back to the whole question of budget cuts to women's centres which are so devastating for women in this country. When we consider the number of centres that have been covered across the country by $1.6 million, it is really a very small amount. As I said earlier, this is one of the most insensitive and inhumane cuts. I do not blame women for feeling that this is the last straw, and that it is actually a direct attack on women and on the women's movement across this country.
A women's centre is a place for women to go when they need support, when things are falling apart at home, when they need to talk to someone who will listen and who will be sympathetic and give encouragement. It is a place to go when they have problems or ideas they want to share, when they have been battered or abused and they just do not know where to go for help. It is a place where they can help others, when they want to volunteer and help their sisters.
Supply
There is so much that women's centres provide, and for such a small, piddling, little amount of money. The value that our society and women themselves have received for the very wonderful service that women's centres across the country provide is incredible.
I want to repeat what everybody on this side of the House has been saying today, and the minister did not seem to hear this morning, that women's centres need core funding. Do we have to keep saying it over and over again? They need basic administrative core funding to pay the rent, to pay for the telephone, to keep the door of the centre open, and to provide, at a very minimum a co-ordinator, who usually works seven days a week and many hours of overtime. The centres are open in the evenings and quite often on the weekends. Emergency services are available. When there is one co-ordinator then you can have many, many volunteers who will help as well. We can multiply the staff that is there to serve people.
I want to pay particular tribute to the women who have worked, and are still struggling to keep women's centres alive across this country.
I met many of them about three years ago when I was on the Secretary of State committee that toured this country several times and spoke to groups in every province. We held hearings because at that time the REAL Women were challenging women's funding of the Secretary of State program. We heard over and over again in every region about how hard women are working, and their dedication to overcome the hassles of having to constantly fight for resources to survive.
The minister and other members opposite have been saying that they would be nice to these poor women by providing fast-tracked project money. As we have been saying over and over again, project money is not the answer. That is not what they want. Project money is of no use if you cannot keep the centre open in the first place and if there is nobody to work with a core of people to develop the programs.
We also know that projects are just adjunct to what centres offer. It is nice to have specialized programs but first the women's centre has to be open and there have to be people there to welcome women and be there to help when women come to their sisters in desperation. You cannot have other programs, as I say, unless first there is core funding to keep it operating.

April 6, 1990
Supply
I think the Secretary of State is really misrepresenting what women's centres want and need. I asked him a number of times today if he had or was going to meet with women in these centres? He said yes. I do not know who he has been meeting with. He would not name any of the groups and he would not say when he had met with them. He certainly would not go to St. John's, Newfoundland, when the women were sitting in at the Secretary of State centre there. In fact, he was the one, through his central office here, who approved police action to go in and not only remove women but to charge them for civil disobedience.
It is incredible. He is the minister who also has refused to go out to British Columbia to meet with women there. They have been protesting and I understand 15 of them were removed forcibly. This is not an isolated policy, it is a policy that has been approved by the minister and it is creating a police state for women in this country. It has got to stop.
When the minister talked about project funding he also neglected to say that this is short-term funding. It is not going to solve tire problem. It takes endless hours of bureaucratic procedure to allocate the money.
Probably one of the poorest communities in Canada is in downtown Vancouver, in an area called the Downtown East Side. The women's centre there, the Downtown East Side Women's Centre, serves the poorest women, street women, women who have come out of mental institutions, women who have alcoholic and drug addiction problems, native women coming from reserves and many of the most troubled women that you can meet. The Secretary of State in the Vancouver region, over and over and over again, refused funding for that centre. I want to put that on the record.
When I hear about all the other centres across the country that have had funding over the years and should have funding, I want to make a particular complaint on behalf of that centre. Yet that is one of the centres that has been writing letters to the editor saying how important centres are in fighting for their sisters.
The minister does not seem to care about this. In fact, I do not think he really even knows about it. Certainly the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, who should be down there in the Downtown East Side talking to these women, could not care less it seems. She
certainly has not given us any indication that she cares or even is beginning to listen to what women are saying.
As I said, we must have a commitment right now to reinstate the funding that the minister took away so brutally for core funding to keep women's centres operating. It amounts to $1.6 million to operate some 75 centres. I am not very good at arithmetic but that certainly does not amount to very much per centre, especially when centres do so very much with such a range of services and ways of helping, and with so many volunteer resources.
Other people have mentioned this as well. It is very hard for Canadians, both men and women, to understand how this government could not just maintain, but increase the funding for CSIS, the security force of Canada, by $33 million.
At the same time, the government cannot find $1.6 million to keep 75 women's centres operating across the country. I think we can see where the government's priorities lie. They prefer to throw women out of Secretary of State offices, to arrest them and to pay for rent-a-cops to protect the Secretary of State offices from these violent women who are attacking them. Actually, these women are conducting civil disobedience in some cases, but certainly to protest the cuts in funding and to demand their rights. I congratulate them for doing this.
This week I asked the minister how much the Secretary of State will be paying for the extra security of these rent-a-cop services that he feels are necessary to protect his staff and to protect his precious files. I know that no women in those offices are interested in getting into files, and they certainly are not interested in attacking staff. Maybe if they could get a hold of the minister, they might like to give him a wallop, but they certainly are not going to pick on people in Secretary of State offices. They were asking for the minister to meet with them, and, of course, this is what he has not done.
I must repeat again, where is the minister responsible for the Status of Women in all of this? She is supposed to be defending Canadian women. She is supposed to be
April 6, 1990

listening to their concerns. She is supposed to be going to the minister and to cabinet on their behalf.
That is the purpose of this office. That is why the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, 20 years ago, insisted that this be a new position. Yet it is really a negative position now. It is incredible that in the one or two times when she has responded in the House, she has just angrily defended the government and its cut-backs. These cut-backs are decimating women's centres.
I heard the minister last night on the news channel. He was again defending his action in cutting core funding for women, and accusing people who did not like this of trivializing and marginalizing women's centres. That is the jargon he has been using. Women are trivializing women's centres by demanding funding to keep them operating. One of the women from British Columbia, from the Vancouver Status of Women, on the same program pointed out that in B.C., 21 centres received $478 from Secretary of State. In addition to fund raising, they provided 61,000 volunteers which valued at over $450,000. It cannot be said that they are not doing their part.
I see that my time is almost up. I just want to again say to women across this land: Keep up the fight. This is a fight for equality. It is just the tip of the iceberg. We must have funds for women's centres reinstated immediately.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, I would like to specify that, since I will share my time with one of my colleagues, I will only use the first 10 minutes.
I am a little confused by the motion before us today. I listened to the speeches made by the Hon. Members for Halifax and Vancouver East and I came to the conclusion that it is hard to change. It was 20 years ago that the Royal Commission on the Status of Women tabled its report.
If I personally asked my colleagues opposite whether Canada has moved toward women's social and economic equality in the last 20 years, I am sure they would both agree that the country and the government have made progress in that direction.
In the last six years, this government has also worked in co-operation with Canadian women to achieve women's equality in every sector, in particular by amending existing legislation, introducing new fiscal initiatives and appointing more women to influential positions. This is where it starts.
Let us take social reform for example. The reform of the Divorce Act and the adoption of certain legislative measures such as the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act have resulted in greater compliance with these orders and agreements. Several provinces have set up a computerized central enforcement machinery which is automatically triggered by the legal system.
To fight against family violence, Madam Speaker, our government has earmarked over a four-year period some $40 million, including $22.2 million which were used to develop 500 new facilities where victims of violence could find temporary shelter, in addition to the 1,400 emergency housing facilities already provided for by the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This assistance makes it possible for 25,000 other women and their children to find shelter and escape violence.
Of course, when we consider the progress made, we are all aware that there is still much to do, but I suggest this is a continuing process. What matters is that the situation is improving and that increased efforts will be made to improve it further.
To fight against family violence, the government has taken other initiatives, for instance in research. A veiy significant point, in view of some real cases, is the new awareness of the legal system. The awareness of the public, the allocation of special funds to native communities, and all the initiatives resulting from the federal legislation which came into force in January 1988 to fight against child and the sexual abuse.
Madam Speaker, the government has implemented other legislation to help and treat more fairly aging women. I refer for instance to the spouses' allowances, the survivors' benefits, as well as the amendments to the Pension Act and the Pension Benefits Standards Act.
April 6, 1990

The purpose of these legislative measures was first and foremost to help women more and more.
Madam Speaker, I suggest everybody will agree that women are playing a more active roll in the economic life of this country and that, as such, they contribute still more to its economic development.
Today women are 44 per cent of the labour force. Statistics show that they account for 73 per cent of Canada's economic growth since 1980. In the last five and a half years, Madam Speaker, our government has done much to remove the obstacles that prevented women from participating fully in our economic life. One of these achievements was the passage of the Employment Equity Act in 1986.
Our government has established an equal-pay program to help federally regulated employers comply with the requirement that everyone be paid the same for work of equal value.
Recently, on January 26, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) announced salary adjustments for some Public Service employees. Under a joint management-labour agreement, about 70,000 public servants in female-dominated occupational groups will receive on average $4,000 each in retroactive payments, as well as annual adjustments of 4 to 7 per cent.
The policies which our government has adopted over its term of office, and I already mentioned several of them, have provided women with greater opportunities to participate more in the economic life of our country and to contribute more to its economic prosperity.
The barriers that prevent people from obtaining better jobs and participating more in society are hard to overcome for some groups, in particular native, immigrant and illiterate women. Our government is continuing to establish policies and programs to eliminate these barriers and to help women prepare for a better future.
For example, to help native women we set up a federal-provincial task force whose mandate is to study the economic development issue and suggest ways to offer them more interesting challenges in business, management and self-development.

After giving serious consideration to the needs and aspirations of women immigrants, we organized a linguistic training program to help them settle in their new country. The program, designed for immigrant women who are not in the labour force and who remain at home to look after their family, proved to be profitable and we decided to expand it. In 1988 our government invested $25 million to help women immigrants get used to life in Canada and improve their employment opportunities by offering basic language courses in their own country, expanding orientation and linguistic training programs in Canada, and offering these women a wider choice of training courses for specific jobs.
To my mind, Madam Speaker, the most constructive initiative taken by the government to give women better opportunities to take part in the various activities of our society has to be the $80 million five-year scholarship program unveiled in 1988 to encourage Canadian students to major in engineering, applied sciences, mathematics, agriculture, physics and biology. At least half of these scholarships will go to women. The contribution of women is essential if we want Canada to compete successfully in tomorrow's world economy, and this program reflects that fact.
Madam Speaker, our government has made a firm commitment to women's equality. Amendments already in place provide a stepping stone towards that goal, and we want to continue to work as a full partner in promoting the right of women to full and equal participation in our society.
We have also focussed on the needs and aspirations of immigrant women. We have set up a language training program.
In view of all those objectives, Madam Speaker, we can say that some things a have been achieved, but that there is still much to be done. And we believe some degree of cooperation is in order. The government program I am the proudest of as a woman is the Scholarship Canada studies fund. If I were sitting on the other side, I would make an effort to consider Bill C-21 and the harm it has done to women. Madam Speaker, as I would like to point out to the hon. member, we all agree that the work done in women's centres is most important. But this area must as any other reflect the changes our society has undergone. Reference was made earlier to progress in some areas. It is a fact that women's groups have contributed a lot to our society's evolution. We now have a co-ed society, which probably was not the case when you were going to school nor indeed when I was; we have a society where boys and girls share the same education system; when you go to a university you find that often female students out number male. If we do not face up to the fact that society has changed over these last 20 years, we will still be addressing the problems of 20 years ago rather than the present ones. We must be able to adopt and to change, we must find new ways to meet those challenges. On a number of occasions today, during Questions Period the minister had this answer: Submit applications! For core funding, applications have bveen made yearly anyway. Test the system, submit your applications. You would not have to
wait long for an answer. We will treat them on a priority basis so that you know exactly where you stand.
It seems to me this is a lot of noise rather than a attempt to find out what this is all about. Is the change so dramatic, or does it allow us not only to identify core needs but also to specify the scope of activity of an individual group?
I was once much involved with consumers'groups. At one time, we reviewed grant programs. I can tell you those programs are very similar to women's programs. However, applications once decided upon must be replaced by others.
As I said earlier: Yes, we have done a lot of things. But we are not ready to say there is nothing else to do. There remains a lot to do. We must move forward, it is imperative that those centres, those groups, keep on working. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure and a privilege for me to speak in the debate this afternoon. The issue of the women's centres has been no more an issue anywhere in the country than in my own community and in my own province.
In Newfoundland and Labrador we have seen the threatening of closure of seven women's centres. At this time in my province they are playing a role that is probably expected of no other women's centres, at least certainly not to the same extent, considering the nature of the economy, the fishery and some of the many other difficult social challenges that we face in coming to grips with some of the realities that we see.
Nobody in our society feels the pressure, takes more of the responsibility and is left with more of the task of keeping a family together, particularly in a society like ours in Newfoundland and Labrador, than the woman. We are seeing in our women's centres and in other places an increased demand for services for the family and for women as our communities come to face and to deal with the realities that are before us.
Over the last little while the women's centres have played a tremendous role, not only the traditional role of advocacy and providing referral services and education, but particularly in providing a base from which women's
April 6, 1990

groups-which are community and family groups-can provide other services either directly or indirectly. The women's centres have played a substantial role in the development of transition houses, crisis intervention centres and programming. They play a tremendous role in providing advice to those who need to know about a community or region as they provide analyses of current social trends, the effects of the economy and how a community is responding and the needs of that community down the road.
The women's centres have played a tremendous role in ensuring that all of us know what it is that matters to women, what is important to women and how their interests are best represented, best addressed and kept in the forefront of the minds of people who make decisions or who do things that impact on women.
Therefore, the ongoing role of these women's centres is clearly essential. This is something that I have made very clear to the Secretary of State. He and I have discussed this matter virtually every day for the last three weeks. I know that he understands the situation in Newfoundland and Labrador.
He has met with me and with the chair of the Provincial Advisory Council on the Status of Women. He has met with me and with the provincial Minister of Education who was representing his colleague who is responsible for the status of women. He has had his officials meet with officials of other departments on the basis of conversations that I and others have had to bring people together.
The point of all that is to bring together the resources of the Government of Canada, the province of Newfoundland and Labrador and the community to ensure that the ongoing support and resources are available so that the women's centres in Newfoundland and Labrador can continue their work.
We can sit around and debate and argue about core funding, about this, that and the other envelope. My concern is that those seven centres are able to continue. They must continue.
I am not going to spend resources and energy banging my head against the wall, when in my view I should be out trying to deal with the situation that we have in front
Supply
of us. That says to me that I, and I know others, including and especially the Secretary of State want to put together those resources so that we can continue the operation of these centres.
We have increased funding in Newfoundland and Labrador. That funding has a much greater flexibility that will allow us to have these facilities continue.
What is essential is that we meet and sit down with officials of the Secretary of State and representatives of the women's centres. The minister has said that he will meet with representatives of the women's centres.
We have seen the effectiveness when dealing with the Second Storey Centre in Bridgewater, a centre that we all know is very effective and has done a tremendous amount of work.
We do have the capacity to make this happen, if we have the will. The need is there. There is no one in my community who disputes that. What we need to do now with the help of the Secretary of State who has made it very clear to me, to this House and to people across the country, and who is prepared to be flexible and move forward with the type of funding that we need, is to ensure that the centres continue. More than anything, it is important to ensure that the centres do continue now and into the future, so that they can continue to provide the services, the voice and the education for women in my province where, sadly, it is still needed as much as ever.

Women are playing key roles in helping to change the fabric of our society in the way that our country is moving and governed.

April 6, 1990

That is a positive statement. I am proud to be part of it.
There is also a segment of our society that needs our help, support, dollars and appropriate legislation because it cannot possibly survive or achieve the status that we would like it to achieve unless we do provide help.
I do not think these women want handouts. Women are not like that. We do not want to be on the dole. But there are some people in society because of their position in life or because of what they have been bom into who have no way out.
The previous speaker from Newfoundland stated that eloquently. He recognizes that in his own riding. I congratulate him for that.
I would like to look at a project in my own riding, the riding of Nepean, which is probably considered fairly affluent. But there is not a riding in this country that does not have depressed people, demoralized and deflated people. People in my riding and I have been trying to get a project going. It is called SWIN, Shelters for Women in Nepean. We have applied through the Minister of Housing for funding for that project. We can get capital funding for a shelter for women in Nepean where our women are having to be transported hundreds of miles away if they have to get out of an unhappy home situation. But there is nothing there to help with the operating costs. The government will help build a shelter, but where will the money for the operating costs come from?
To get to the cuts of $1.6 million, I wonder if the the person who was there with that big sharp knife cutting the money from these projects really looked and saw who they were hurting. It is not you or me, not us here in the House. They are hurting the women who can least afford to be hurt. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, I will comment if I may on my hon. friend's comment. One of the problems and the frustrations that we have in a province like Newfoundland and Labrador is that there are a tremendous number of services that need to be provided. But either because the provincial government has its priorities in a certain order, or because it does not have the resources, these services cannot be or are not being provided. That happens with eveiy provincial government in Atlantic Canada. It has nothing to do with parties or anything. That is just the way it is.
As well, the community is often not at the point of being able to provide a service. Needs emerge in smaller communities in rural Atlantic Canada. They have a long way to come compared to Nepean. I think my friend recognizes that.
What we have seen is that out of necessity one way or another, or because of a clear commitment, women's centres have provided a tremendous base of services to women and families, partly in the absence of other people being able to do it and partly, as I say, the commitment is there.
There is no question that we must continue to support women and women's programs directed to those people in our society in the sector that my friend was referring to who need the help the most. Tragically, so many of those problems befall on people simply because they are women. That is something that we must continue to work against in this country. Despite the great accomplishments that we on this side talk about, and which my friend acknowledges, women, simply because they are women, have a tremendous number of problems that the other half of us do not simply because we are men. In this country, that is wrong. It is not something that you change by law, sadly. It is something that you change by attitude.
In terms of commitment, this government has been committed to women in a number of ways. Hon. members have heard about it. I want to talk briefly about one program that we funded through ACOA.
Some $800,000-odd was allocated to develop a women's enterprise centre, to provide women a source of information so that they could start businesses, recognizing that women are under-represented in the business community in Newfoundland and that their capacity is not being developed, enhanced or released so that we can see economic development and job creation.
ACOA put in that amount of money to say: "Let's go. Let's see what is out there. Let's say to women, 'Come in. What ideas do you have? We will help you around the red tape.'" It is not money. It is not source funding. It is not grants or anything else. It is: "We'll tell you how to get other sources of money, what the red tape is, where
April 6, 1990

the comers are and we will help you cut them." The commitment is there.
Family violence is another area. We are focusing on the illiteracy of women.
There are a lot of things in my province that we have been able to do, but an awful lot more has to be done.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all human beings are bom free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood. That is the first article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
I would like to stress the terms "dignity" and "brotherhood". In an increasingly violent society, where the number of the homeless and the needy is increasing, where can we find this spirit of community and brotherhood? In women's centres or, at least, in the few centres that will survive the budget cuts imposed by the Conservative government.
This is the second year the government has drastically cut back on funding for women's centres. It has entirely abolished core funding for organizations that meet a vital need in all communities. These centres, where the majority of the staff are volunteers, were created to respond to emergencies, but this government has said no, no more!
These centres are often the first place where battered women, alone or with their children, go to get some human warmth, assistance, information and especially support, in a crisis situation. Now there is no more funding to help these centres stay open, who will be there? Who will take over? Who will be on call 24 hours a day?
The unemployment rate is rising and, as was announced by the Minister of Finance, will continue to do so. This will only aggravate social unrest, aggressive behavior and poverty. As of next January, the GST will put additional pressure on all those women who already have trouble making ends meet. Where can they go? Where will they turn?
Supply
More than 40 women's centres in Quebec alone will be forced to close because the government has cut $1.6 million in aid programs for women. And that, while they are often the sole bread winner. If we refuse to help them, how can they help their children?
And what about the large number of children who lack the very basics, who through these centres were getting some form of assistance and especially an environment that was less disturbed than what they were exposed to daily. All these children living in substandard housing and raised in an climate of despair and violence are the foundation of our society, but the government is abandoning them by cutting funding for women's programs.
Is this how this government intends to prepare our young people for the future, by forcing them into a life of misery early on? Is it trying to show how unimportant the future of this country is, since they are our future and will soon take our places?
Madam Speaker, I know full well that the Secretary of State will answer me that they will support at least 600 projects totalling $6 million, as he told us on March 26. However, he added, and I quote:
I realize there are areas where far more should be done, including
Native women, women who belong to visible minorities, immigrant
women and, of course, women living in isolated rural areas.
Since the Minister admits that far more should be done, how can he justify a $1.6 million cut to the Women's Program? The needs are obvious, often urgent, and this money is essential for some 75 centres. It is a matter of life or death for them and the Conservative government is condemning them to death, just to get back $1.6 million. We see how important the human factor is when it comes to money! How sad!
Mr. Speaker, the government managed to add $114 million to the budget for the Canadian Armed Forces in Europe, while the eastern countries are gradually opening up. It was able to find $33 million more for the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. However, it was not able to keep, let alone increase, $1.6 million for the Women's Program. What a curious way to handle a budget.

Women's organizations have been providing for next to nothing the types of information and services which would cost provincial governments millions of dollars to take on. With the budget presented by the Conservative government not so long ago, how are the provinces going

April 6, 1990
Supply
to find the resources to pick up the tab? Who will be losing in the end? Women and children-society as a whole.
What about the Canada Assistance Plan, CAP, which funds social assistance, but which also provides shelters for battered women? With the Tories slapping a spending limit on the three provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario, what will happen to women in need?
Presently, shelters for battered women must turn away one out of every two women who come to them desperate for a place to feel secure in. Where will they go? What will happen to them? Does the government need that $1.6 million so badly?

Mr. Speaker, when I asked the Minister responsible for the Status of Women if she had good news for women's groups in Canada, and I would really like to have some this afternoon, she answered, "As the Secretary of State said, we are looking for a solution. He is prepared to release emergency funds to help these organizations apply for project funding."
I do not understand why, if the minister is prepared to release funds, he has to wait for an emergency. Can this government not do prevention instead of picking up the pieces? The solution it is looking for is so obvious: it only has to assure the women's centres of the money it intends to take from them. Is it not better to invest in something that works well than to have to start all over again in a crisis? Surely, without great effort, we could find a way to help the 75 centres stay open and continue their extremely useful work. When we take into account the efforts devoted by hundreds of volunteers and the help given to thousands of women at a critical time in their lives, we realize that $1.6 million is not much.
Who will be there when the next crisis occurs? The police? The emergency services? Canadian women are not asking the government that much. Don't they contribute their fair share? Why refuse them a little support when they are in dire need?
With the new legislation concerning RRSPs, the conservative government will give a tax break to people earning more than $86,000 a year that will cost the public Treasury a further $400 million dollars, and the same government has the gall to argue that it must cut $1.6
million in the Women's Program. Is that a way to meet the real needs of Canadians?
Mr. Speaker, we are gearing for year 2000 but we forget to prepare those who will be living in the next century. In 1990, the Tory government promised a higher unemployment rate, it cut funding of the Women's Program and capped Canada Assistance Plan contributions in British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario.
Result: In each of the three provinces where a ceiling has been put on CAP benefits there will be no place for more than 50,000 children in day care centres. Has the government any suggestions for parents-single parents in most instances-who had planned to send their kids there?
Result: At least 75 women's homes will have to close down for lack of money. Whom will battered and desperate women turn to in times of crisis? The police?
Result: Ever more women are unable to land a job, but when they do find work they have nobody to look after their children. Who will offer them financial security? The welfare system!
It is a sad comment on our society when the government cuts off essential services and then spends $14 million to promote the goods and services tax which nobody wants and which will only swell the ranks of poor Canadians. Under such circumstances they find it increasingly difficult to keep their dignity and maintain a spirit of brotherhood.
Nothing warrants the $1.6 million cut-back which will force so many women's centres to close down. They exist because they meet a real need which nobody else wanted to meet. They exist because our society is not all that well. They exist because in many instances they faced up to critical situations which others would not even acknowledge. And now the government wants to get rid of them to save a paltry $1.6 million.
Has anybody measured the cost in human failures which will result from the closing of these centres? Has anybody considered its social impact? Has anybody suggested an alternative to face up to the critical situation which will result from this closing? And above all, can anyone explain the logic behind these cut-backs
April 6, 1990

which, while helping nobody, create hardship for the have-nots in our society.

Mr. Speaker, the more I search, the less I find the logic in a $1.6 million cut, forcing 75 centres for women throughout Canada to close. In a period of Canadian life when tensions are high, poverty is on the rise, violence and crime are daily news and jobs are getting rarer by the minute, we need centres. We need centres for women to help them get through the crisis.
These centres ask government for a minimum. Daily, volunteers are there as a help, as a presence, as counsellors, with time to give and no pay to take. These are the centres the Tories are closing. This is the saving, $1.6 million, that will save the budget?

Why is the government so determined to keep women and their children live in misery? What have they said to deserve such a wrath? Is the government demonstrating his lack of consideration for Canadian women by aban-donning them in times of crisis? Is it because they never lived through such desperate situations that none of the members on the government side can sympathize with this cause and defend it. Yet, it is not necessary to have experienced every kind of hardship to support such a worthy project. Could it be that this Tory Government has doubts about the usefulness of these women's centres? Could it be the unavowed reason behind these cuts?
Article 4 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: "No one shall be held in slavery or servitude; slavery and the slave trade shall be prohibited in all their forms."
Mr. Speaker, slavery and servitude become the destiny of all the battered women who do not know where to go. It is the destiny of all those who have become homeless against their will. It is the fate of all the have-nots who seem to go through a series of critical situations. As a society, what are we going to do?
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I cannot accept the many excuses the Conservative government comes up with when asked to give back $1.6 million, an amount that should not ruin it, to the Equal Opportunities for
Supply
Women Program. It would thus allow 75 women's centres to continue to deal with crisis situations.
Mr. Speaker, when women ask for help, the government must be totally responsive and support them. That is why I ask once again that the $1.6 million be reinstated immediately to preserve what is in place.

Madam Speaker, before I start I would like to say that my 20 minutes is going to be shared by my colleague across.
I would like to make a few comments in addressing the motion before this House. The first has to do with the difficulty of bringing this country's deficit under control.
All members of this House are acutely aware that this government is saddled with an enormous debt. We are managing a debt which threatens our existing social programs. But, worse, unless this debt is reduced now there will simply be no hope of our expanding these programs or even contemplating new and needed social programs.
The Minister of Finance and this government are reducing the nation's debt. We have done what had to be done to bring government spending under control. We have started the deliberate task of building toward balanced budgets. It is only when fiscal stability is in sight that we will be able to consider the different social programs which Canada needs.
Yes, we have had to reduce spending in some areas. It was not a pleasure making those reductions. Let no one think otherwise. They were not made because we wanted to make them. They were made because we had to make them.
No reduction is popular. Everyone has a vested interest in some aspect of federal spending and they complain bitterly when that spending is reduced. No one wants their program to be touched.
The reductions we have seen are to areas in which we can no longer afford to participate, or in which we have to move more slowly, or in which other jurisdictions have a more rightful place.
Every member of this House acknowledges that there are women in need of help: women whose lives have been tom by violence against them, women who have been abandoned by their mates, or women whose lives have been disadvantaged. Every member will agree that women's centres provide that help, that they are there for women.
Supply
However, every province in this country provides social services to people in need. These social services provide necessary information, provide referral to appropriate agencies, and provide support and counselling. These are provincial services so one may reasonably ask: Why was the federal government supporting another system of services?
Through the Canada Assistance Plan the federal government supports one-half of provincial expenditures on social services for women and other populations. Over the years the federal government has invested heavily in the core funding of women's centres. It no longer can afford to do so and provinces will have to assume more responsibility. However, note that the federal government will share one-half of whatever provinces spend on services for women in need.
As I noted earlier, there are many ways in which women are in need. We have all become acutely aware of the need for more and better child care. It was this government which was the first to do something to address that need. We wanted to do more and members opposite will recall how we were prevented from doing so by the other place. We all now wish that all elements of the national strategy on child care had been put in place. Not all were, and now we find ourselves having to go slower on child care than planned as we manage the nation's debt. However, both the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have stated on numerous occasions that a national child care program will be operational before the end of this mandate.
This strategy will enhance the well-being of families and children in terms of meeting child care needs. This will affect families all across the country, but some elements were put in place and they are directly helping women across Canada every day of the year.
The federal government has, as part of the national strategy on child care, implemented two major initiatives on child care. In this regard families now have access to enhanced tax assistance for pre-school aged children through an enriched child care expense deduction which was doubled to $4,000 per child in 1988 and a new $200 supplement to the child tax credit. Ihken together, these measures assist almost two million families. In addition, a child care initiatives fund has also been established to encourage innovation and enhance the development of approaches and services as they relate to child care issues by providing funding to projects that promote

April 6, 1990
Supply
quality child care services for Canadian families. Women who must work have more affordable child care because of these measures.
The child care initiatives fund, which is just two years old, has had a profound impact on child care in this country. The government has already committed over $33 million in support of some 250 projects across Canada. Members will recall that priorities of the initiatives fund included the stimulation of services within native communities for special needs children, in rural and remote communities for parents who work part time or on shifts, and within multicultural communities.
All of these needs are being addressed. Let us acknowledge the facts. These are the needs of women. These are the needs of women who must work or whose child care arrangements make work difficult and complex. Addressing these needs lets women participate economically and equally. It helps women obtain the training and education which they need to enter and rise in the labour force.
Let us look at just a few of the projects being supported by the child care initiatives fund. In Montreal the Board of Trade is stimulating employer supported child care. It is persuading its members to develop services for employees. In Langruth, Manitoba the Lakeview Children's Centre is developing child care services for farm women of that community. Big city and small town, women's child care needs are being addressed.
In Edmonton the Franciscan Sisters have established multicultural services to support parents while they establish themselves in this new land. The Family Service Bureau in Regina will provide emergency services for sick children to assist working parents.
Projects to provide care to children after school until their parents are off work are being undertaken in Fort St. John, B.C. and Windsor, Ontario. Groups in Kent County, New Brunswick and Red Lake, Ontario are designing services which let handicapped children be cared for with other children.
Perhaps most gratifying of all is the success of the child care initiatives fund in assisting Indian and Inuit communities in the design and development of child care. Some
20 per cent of its projects have been awarded to our native peoples. Who more than our Indian and Inuit women deserve help? The initiatives fund is helping.
These are all demonstration projects. They are to test new and better ways of caring for children. Clearly the parents of the children served by these projects will benefit but, in time as other communities see what can be and has been done, the parents and their children in those communities will benefit. Most of all, the women of Canada will benefit.
While the motion before us would have you believe, Madam Speaker, that this government does not care about women, it is quite clear that we have initiated programs which are very much for the benefit of Canadian women. In these tight economic times we have had to make choices. We have chosen to support women and children.
