Therefore, we are arguing semantics, which is unfortunate because it does take up an awful lot of Parliament's time. Unfortunately, that seems to be the way it is.
I know that there are some members who were not with us earlier when there was this outbreak that caused those of us on the government side no doubt to sit with a smile on our faces at the conflict that appeared to be between the members of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party. It was an exchange, a series of mea culpas. I was there first, whose on second, what's his name is on third. Fortunately, it did not go on but it did seem to break the strain that seemed to be in evidence at the time.
That seems to be over, but I notice that there are two very strong voices in the Liberal party who no doubt will not let me go unscathed after I sit down. It is their job and I can see from the expression on their faces that it will be their absolute delight and pleasure and there will be a few more pleasures down at the other end of the Chamber as well. With that brief assessment of how I view where we have taken ourselves so far today, I wish to express that it is with pleasure that I have the opportunity to speak to the opposition motion concerning the reinstatement of funds to women's centres.
Madam Speaker, I want members of this House to know that we, the government, have had a longstanding interest in promoting the health and well-being of Canadian women. The federal government carries out, as you well know, a variety of programs that address the particular needs of women. In recent years, we have developed new initiatives such as the one to prevent family violence, to respond to the concerns that women themselves have told us are important to them.
Family violence is an issue of tremendous concern to women and to Canadian society generally. We estimate that between one in ten to one in eight women each year are physically abused by the men they live with. This means that as many as one million Canadian women each year are being abused by their husbands or partners. We also know that the majority of victims of child sexual abuse and abuse of the elderly are women. The Badgley Commission reported in 1984 that half of all young women have experienced some form of sexual abuse.
These figures are horrific. Ten years ago, we as a society were largely unaware of the seriousness and extent of this problem. Since that time, it has been women themselves who have worked long and hard to bring to light the problems of family violence and violence against women. This government has vowed to help them.
The federal government through the Department of National Health and Welfare and other departments has worked and worked hard to support women's groups in creating greater public awareness of these issues. We have supported public education programs, national and regional conferences, training initiatives and research studies to create greater public awareness of the causes and consequences of family violence. During this time we have worked closely and consulted with many women's organizations and services all across this country.
The federal government is and remains committed to working with Canadian women to create a society where women do not have to fear for their personal security and lives, either at home or in public. To this end, the federal government announced in June, 1988 a new federal initiative on family violence. This initiative, which is currently under way, has a budget of $40 million over a four-year period and involves 14 federal departments carrying out measures to address family violence. The Department of National Health and Welfare plays the lead role in co-ordinating this initiative.
Under this initiative, we are seeking to better co-ordinate existing federal activities on family violence, to augment these with new activities and to create better means of co-operation among federal departments, provincial and territorial governments and NGOs.
We are working on a number of fronts to prevent and reduce family violence. For example, we are supporting front line voluntary organizations that help women affected by family violence. We are developing new approaches to policing and enforcement. We are supporting research studies on better ways to treat offenders, providing services to native communities experiencing family violence. As well, we are supporting the training and education of professions to better equip them to recognize and deal with family violence. We are also working to develop, in consultation with provincial and territorial governments, provincial associations,
April 6, 1990

business and non- governmental organizations, a concerted long term strategy to address family violence.
I do not think there is anyone in this House who has not had or heard of some kind of example of how much work remains to be done in the area of violence against women. My wife works in a related area and her work there has taught me much. Exposure to the problem has convinced me how important this work is and how necessary it is.
In the case of one pregnant teenage student in my wife's program, the teenager was pregnant for a second time. The pregnancy was caused by her father who, when the teenager indicated that she was going to the police, was struck on the head by the father with a baseball bat. She now suffers from a permanent lingering side effect of this assault. When she was asked why she and her mother did not leave, she answered that as rough as it was at home, it was the only home that they had.
New initiatives are required. One of the most significant elements of these initiatives is a new program called Project Haven which is providing $22 million over four years to increase the number of emergency shelter units or rooms for battered women and their children across Canada. Emergency shelters are an essential resource for battered women and their children. They provide short term accommodation and a safe haven for women and their children who have had to flee an abusive home. Research indicates that a typical victim of such abuse will have been beaten an average of 35 times before she seeks help. Emergency shelters, as well as providing much needed protection, also provide a supportive environment, counselling and information on the options available to women to deal with the problem of abuse.
Project Haven is managed by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation on behalf of the Department of National Health and Welfare and contributes up to 100 per cent of the capital cost of constructing new shelters. The cost of operating the shelters after they are built will be shared between provincial governments and the federal government. We have agreed that provincial governments approve new shelters before we proceed with capital funding under Project Haven and we have established co-ordinating mechanisms with our provincial counterparts to set shelter priorities and to review funding applications. We have placed priority on serving
Supply
areas which are especially underserviced in emergency shelter facilities and we will give priority to special client groups such as disabled, immigrant, rural and native women.
By the end of the four-year initiative, in March of 1992, we expect to have created an additional 500 new units for battered women. We estimate that these new shelter units will accommodate about 25,000 additional women and children per year on an ongoing basis.
To date, federal officials have negotiated final arrangements with their provincial counterparts for the construction of 301 new shelter units under this program. Project Haven represents a significant undertaking by the federal government to address the needs of Canadian women who have been victimized by violence. It is an example of the kind of co-operative undertaking we have been developing under the family violence initiative where we have worked closely with provincial-territorial governments and community women's groups. Under the current initiative, we have responded to the most immediate needs such as emergency shelter of abused women. We have also undertaken a process of consultation and planning with other government and non-government organizations to develop a long term, national approach to preventing family violence.
We expect that many of these longer term initiatives will become integrated into the ongoing activities of federal departments. We intend to continue our initiatives to prevent and reduce family violence and to continue to consult and work with women's organizations in this process.
As I noted earlier, family violence and other forms of violence against women remain a major concern and priority of women's groups and individual women across this country. Preventing such violence and obtaining full equality for Canadian women will also remain a major concern and priority of this government.

Some of the programs they brag about, you should really take a look at. They talk about the family violence program on which they are going to spend $40 million over four years. That amounts of $10 per battered woman per year.
There was a lot of discussion from the previous speaker about Project Haven. It was supposed to provide 500 beds. Two years later it has provided 49 beds.
At the same time, in the last budget they introduced a limit on Canada Assistance Plan funding, which will limit the operating cost expenditures in provinces like Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
I have heard talk from the government about employment equity. Since this government has come to power, the wage gap between men and women has increased. When they came into government, women were receiving 66 per cent of the average wage of men. They are now receiving 65 per cent. It has been reduced. Yes, there are some very high profile women, including cabinet ministers, but the average working woman in this country is worse off.
They talk about pay equity in terms of the public service. Yet the government stalled for five years on pay equity and then only offered one quarter of what they were entitled to.
They have talked about language training for immigrant women. The government has not eliminated the inherent discrimination against women in government language training programs. Why did the government eliminate the settlement language training program that mostly affects women? It talks as if it is improving things, but then it eliminates one of the most effective programs, the language settlement training program that was mainly used by immigrant women.
It talks about native women. Well, I do not understand how any member of this government can get up and talk about native women, when it has just cut $9.8 million from native programs.
The most laughable one is when it starts talking about child care. This government promised and promised child care, and once it gets elected it withdrew all its promises and is now trying to suck the Canadian people in so that it can promise it again.
There have been problems in my own municipality with loss of child care spaces, loss of basic child care. It is veiy nice to have initiative programs which would be icing on the cake, if there was any cake. In my own municipality of Surrey, the women's centre-I could not possibly be out of time already.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will certainly put my question. The previous speaker stated that this was all a matter of semantics. In my own municipality of Surrey in South Surrey-White Rock, the women's centre's core funding was reduced by $25,000. They have had to close their sexual abuse program, their battered wives program, and they are going to be able to keep the doors open by bingos and casinos. I ask the member whether he thinks that is a matter of semantics.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the less than one minute that I am allowed to respond, I have made points on about six or seven items that my hon. colleague made reference to. I only wish I had the opportunity to address each and every one them, because certainly I could. I will respond to two in the very brief period of time that remains.
With respect, I am totally appalled at his example of our efforts being made only in areas that affect high quality or high status women. On the one hand, if there is not some acknowledgement being placed towards the very significant and real contribution that women can make in positions of so-called status, our efforts are deemed to be useless and worthless because they are, after all, not meaningful.
On the other hand, I can cite many examples and cases of situations where I have personally been involved representing the Government of Canada where our efforts have been made by and large at numbers of people who are suffering from a broad perspective of problems.
April 6, 1990

The very last item the hon. member raises is the one about semantics. The difference between operating funds and program funds is, in a nutshell, the difference between having an organization that is responsible and accountable for its funds, as all members in the House of Commons must be, as opposed to those who are not. Simply to disburse a pailful of operational funds at a business location with an address and expect that it will do good things is not good enough for the people of Canada.
They have told us that they want all such funding sources to be truly accountable and responsible to the people of Canada. It is therefore to that degree, in that extent, that the hon. Minister of State, I think rightly, has made money available on a project by project basis.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do want to talk about these semantics which the previous speaker brought forward. It seems that a great deal of words have been put around the issue by the government, because it chooses not to address the issue.
The issue is women's centres, centres operated by women and for women. The issue is $1.6 million that the government has chosen to cut completely so that those centres have no federal funding. The issue is, will the government, or will it not, recognize its obligations to give women the ability to speak for themselves, to decide for themselves what programs and what services they need. Will the government restore the $1.6 million? That is the issue on the table today.
The government members so far have chosen not to speak to that issue. They have talked a great deal about what they have done for women. In the last three years funding for women's programs has dropped from $13 million to $9 million. It is a simple fact of life that with dollars in your pocket or in your bank account, you can accomplish something and without them, you cannot.
The government, not only by this year's cuts to the women's centres, but by last year's cuts to women's programs, again a matter of 15 per cent, has chosen to stifle the voices of women, to cripple their ability to gain equity in Canadian society. It is doing it not only through the women's programs. It is also doing it through having allowed the Court Challenges Program to lapse and giving it nothing but a temporary, interim amount of
Supply
funding to carry on. What that has done is completely thwart the efforts of many organizations to bring to the courts the issues that are constraining women's equality, to attempt through the courts to firmly establish women's rights under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The attack on women, women's programs and on women's rights is not limited to the total cancellation of funding for women's centres in 75 communities across Canada. It is happening throughout government programs.
It seems to me that perhaps members opposite need to be reminded what the women's centres do. Fundamentally, they empower women and allow women to come together to determine their needs, to gain knowledge, confidence and the skills that they need to function fully in Canadian society whether that be as mothers staying at home, as grandmothers, as young girls growing up, as women entering the workforce or as women still in the workforce. That is what the government wants to cut, the ability of women to establish themselves clearly and unequivocally as full participants in all aspects of Canadian society.
Lest people think that there is no need for that, women have arrived and are sitting here in the House of Commons in miniscule numbers, but nonetheless they are here and we do not need to do anything more for women. I think that is the tenor of some of the discussions I have heard today.
I want to remind the members of the House that for many decades the status of women was determined on an 1876 precedent of British common law that ruled that women are persons in matters of pains and penalties, but not persons in matters of rights and privileges.
Every October, the women in this House and other women get together to celebrate the personhood of women that was decided in 1929. The personhood of women was never decided by a court in Canada. It was decided by the Privy Council in Britain. The last pronouncement of the Canadian courts on women as persons per se, was the following: "That since persons required for the public office must be fit and qualified, only men would be eligible for appointment to the

April 6, 1990
Supply
Senate". They were ruling specifically on a request that women be defined as persons.
I want to talk very briefly about some of the indicators that women still are far from equal participants in society, that the disadvantages that any person can suffer in society are suffered double, triple or quadruple and more by women.
One in four women in Canada can expect to be sexually assaulted at some time, half of them before the age of 17. A million Canadian women are abused by their husbands or live-in partners every year. Fifty-six per cent of women do not feel safe walking around their neighbourhoods in an urban environment.
Over 42,000 women stayed in crisis shelters in 1985, with 55,000 children. I ask, as we think about women, that we remember that for the large part, women and children are still a unit. Children are the responsibility of women. While there may be some single parent fathers caring for children, the vast majority of children with only one parent are the responsibility solely of women.
What happens to those families? In the first place, if you were in a family headed by a woman, you were five times as likely to be poor than if you were in a family headed by a man. You were only one-quarter as likely to complete high school and go on to university, if you came from that kind of a family.
I want to put in a few statistics about the record of women and their economic status since this government has come to power. In 1984, two-thirds of all poor seniors were women. We hoped that was changing and that we were recognizing the poverty of women as a serious, social and economic crisis and moving towards improving it. But, no, in the last five years it has changed from two-thirds of all poor seniors being women to three-quarters of all poor seniors being women. In case the members opposite are not terribly good at mathematics, that is an increase from 66 per cent to 75 per cent of all poor are women.
I want to talk about why the women's centres fill an important role. The fact is that women experience life in our society differently than men do. There is very little in the public policy structure or in government that recognizes that. How often in the House do we see a male colleague stand up and address any area of their responsibility from the perspective of how a policy or a program or a budget decision affects women?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext: It depends on which party.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CENTRES
speechtext:
Only yesterday, I had to send a note down to the party on my far left to remind one of their key spokespersons that when he talked about the impact of free trade on businessmen, he was excluding one-third of the business people and the businesses in this country. It depends on which party, the member said. Ignorance and neglect of women's issues exists in all parties.
It is not only on the front of the women's centres where there have been cuts. Multicultural programs have been cut which will mean the closing of many heritage language schools and it is certainly going to mean the reduction of heritage language schools. Those heritage language schools are the vehicle through which many women are involved in a meaningful way with the rest of their community.
We are cutting funding to native programs, affecting the ability of natives to communicate with each other and to advocate on their own behalf. Members opposite should know that if you happen to be a woman from a multicultural background or a woman from an aboriginal background, you are doubly discriminated against and in double jeopardy.
I want to know why the minister responsible for this program sits there today and talks about project funding. I heard a very paternalistic attitude in that which says basically: "We know best what is good for you girls out there. Just be good little girls and tell us what you want to do with your money, and we will let you have it". The government will not acknowledge that women's centres, run by women for women, are a good thing because they give power to women to make decisions for themselves and to set their own course in life. The government says: "We will tell you what is good for you and we will let you have some money, if you are good little girls and behave yourselves".
I want to know why women have been arrested in St. John's and charged with public mischief for demonstrating quietly in a federal government office. They were sitting there quietly and making their presence known, nothing more, and they were charged with public mischief. Well, the public mischief is the Secretary of State.
Why are we so afraid of women quietly expressing their opinion that we lock government offices against
April 6, 1990

them? Are they such a threat? The building owner, in whose halls women were demonstrating, did not choose to call the police. He did not find them an interference. He did not find public mischief, but their own government did.
I read into the record earlier and I am going to do it again, the kinds of choices that this government has made when it comes to cutting money and the kinds of choices it has made about where to increase its spending. The Halifax office for visiting cabinet ministers, $1.6 million dollars. That is the same amount that is now being taken away from 75 women's centres across Canada. Boeing Corporation, $161 million, 100 times the amount required to keep all the women's centres in Canada open. Then the increase in the National Defence budget,$560 million: one-third of 1 per cent of that increase would keep all the women's centres in Canada fully funded to the extent they are now. Ceremonial state activities was allocated a $3 million increase. I
